speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present to the House this morning a number of petitions that have been certified correct pursuant to Standing Order 36. The petitioners are from throughout northwestern British Columbia, from Terrace, Prince Rupert, Kitimat, the Hazeltons and other communities who are expressing concerns about the proposed goods and services tax. They believe that this tax should not proceed and that the government should cease with the proposal which would shift the tax burden on to ordinary Canadians through a regressive consumption tax instead of through real tax reforms.

Mr. Speaker, it is also my pleasure to present a petition to this House signed by over 1,000 Canadians, most of whom are students at the Mount Allison University in Sackville, New Brunswick. They call upon their elected representatives to stop the erosion of quality and accessibility in our universities, colleges and other post-secondary educational institutions in Canada.
The petitioners are quite concerned that Bill C-33, introduced in the House on June 27, will reduce federal transfer payments for post-secondary education by approximately $900 million over five years and they respectfully call upon the government to withdraw Bill C-33.

Mr. Speaker, I have a petition, signed by a number of people, with regard to the VIA Rail issue. In this petition these people, many of whom are Canadians, avail themselves of their ancient and undoubted right to present a petition in front of the House of Commons. They believe that the railway passenger service as carried on by VIA Rail is an essential means of transportation for many Canadians and has been part of the basic Canadian infrastructure for over 100 years. They believe that the government's announcement of a $400 million cutback over five years will hurt the industry and they believe it is very important for tourism.
I would like to explain that this petition has been signed by Canadians from Wabowden, Churchill, Gillam, Lundar, Winnipeg, Thompson, Rankin Inlet, Flin Flon, Rexdale, Ontario, and also by non-Canadians from Sweden, Greece, Germany and England.

Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure and privilege to submit a petition to this House pursuant to Standing Order 36. The attached petition is certified as correct in format and content and is from many Canadians of Eglinton-Lawrence and the greater metropolitan area. All of them pray that this House put aside the GST proposals because they see in the GST proposals a tax that will encourage a greater number of cash transactions and lead to greater scoffing of the law and will begin to classify many Canadians in those categories of those who will start to evade as well as avoid paying tax.

Mr. Speaker, I have the honour and the privilege today to present a petition, properly signed by the residents of Thunder Bay, who plead with this government to reconsider their orders to cancel VIA Rail passenger rail service through the city of Thunder Bay.

October 31, 1989

Mr. Jim Fulton (Skeena) moves:
That this House calls upon the Government to implement an
ecologically sound "green" tax system.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have today as a votable day with the motion before the House, calling upon the government to implement an ecologically sound green tax system.
Many members of the House, and certainly many Canadians, will wonder just exactly what that is. The green tax system, the GTS, as we call it, we believe is the way of the future. It proposes to make a new system out of the best of our options either technologically or in terms of the workforce in terms of the natural resources that our country has. The GST, on the other hand, the goods and services tax as proposed by the Minister of Finance, is an admission of failure. It proposes to make a failing system more expensive.
The government says that it endorses the concept of sustainable development, the government says that it wants to integrate economic concerns in all aspects of its policy making, and the government says that it cares about the environment. The government says that it endorses the Brundtland report, the World Commission on the Environment and Development, yet one of the most important doctrines in this report is that economic and environmental processes are inseparable.
It is with amazement and disbelief that we watch this government go backwards in time as it proposes a Draconian tax measure that only serves to compound and amplify our current environmental crisis. The GST is regressive. It taxes recycled paper at the same rate as unrecycled paper, bicycles at the same rate as cars, canoes at the same rates as motor boats, alternative energy at the same rate as fossil fuels.
October 31, 1989

The GST is not just environmentally neutral, it is environmentally damaging. Environmentally sound products often cost more than products that are sustainable. The GST only widens this gap, making it more difficult for consumers to choose greener products. As we have learned in a number of recent polls that have been done by Angus Reid and by others across this country, Canadians are prepared to pay more taxes for certain objectives. The number one objective of Canadians from coast to coast is to have a cleaner, safer, sustainable environment.
The conservative approach of the Minister of Finance, as he admits himself, is to regressively tax workers, the middle class, the poor and small business, to tax transactions, to replace the manufacturers' sales tax with the 9 per cent GST. Many Canadians are wondering why 9 per cent. That is obviously a targeted amount which the Minister of Finance wants to raise for other purposes. The reason the minister has chosen 9 per cent to flog is so that he can bring the rate down to a lower one, then ratchet it back up again and look as though he has done some kind of honourable deed in lowering the tax from nine to eight to seven to six or to five only to ratchet it back up again as was done with the manufacturers' sales tax which went from 9 to 10 to 11 to 12 and continues progressively upwards.
The Conservative and Liberal approach to taxation is identical. If one looks at the last three decades of ministers of finance from both the Liberal and Conservative Parties, we now see the results. Corporations three decades ago paid 50 per cent of the taxes in this country and working families paid 50 per cent. Now corporations pay only 20 per cent and working families pay 80 per cent of the taxes in Canada. Most wealthy Canadians pay little or no tax and thousands of profitable corporations pay little or no tax as well.
We have to ask some fundamental questions such as where does such a tax system lead. The evidence is now overwhelming in Canada. We are among the most polluting and wasteful countries in the world. We learned just this morning in the environment committee from witnesses from Environment Canada that each Canadian produces more than four tonnes of carbon dioxide as a result of our activities in driving cars, through industry and through the various forms of
Supply
carbon dioxide production which are adding to global warming through the production of greenhouse gases.
We are passing on huge fiscal and environmental debts to future generations. One does not need to look far in our environment to find the kinds of huge costs, whether it is the hundreds of billions in national debt to the kinds of debts that are being passed on through poor fishery and forestry practices, the erosion of farmland and the many other problems we have with toxic and hazardous waste dump sites across the country.
The simple fact is that we cannot produce laws, regulations inspectors or courts fast enough to halt, prosecute and clean up the colossal messes that are about us. The list is long. There is acid rain. There is toxic rain. There is Great Lakes pollution. There are holes in the ozone layer. There are greenhouse gases and global warming, toxic and hazardous waste dumps, PCBs, pesticides, nuclear waste, enough low-level radioactive waste and tailing ponds and impoundments to cover the highway from Halifax to Vancouver six feet deep.
The list is long and growing. How often do we now hear of endangered species and endangered spaces in Canada? We need a tax system that is fundamentally simple, ecologically sound and designed to encourage sustainable development. This tax approach will create jobs, reduce resource waste, clean up the environment and pass on to future generations as good a planet as we inherited, the fundamental premise on which the Brund-tland recommendations were made through the United Nations to the world.
How does a green tax system work? It is best, in my view, to deal with examples so that the public has as clear an idea as possible about what a green tax system is all about.
One could ask a question in relation to recycled paper. The question would be, what is the maximum amount of virgin paper that can be reasonably recovered and delivered for recycling. One could take any city, any urban area and in fact many rural areas of the country and ask how many packages, newspapers, and paper are out there and in terms of the costs of gathering and transporting that to a centralized depot near enough to a facility that can de-ink and recycle that paper. As we have learned in some cities on this continent including

October 31, 1989
Supply
some cities right here in Canada, a very substantial amount can be recovered for that form of recycling.
Then you ask what is the maximum amount of recycled fibre that can be reasonably placed in various kinds of products. We know, for example, that the Minister of Public Works, whom I am glad to see here today, produced a Householder made out of recycled paper that had roughly 50 per cent recycled fibre in it. It is good quality paper, it provides legible type, it can carry the reproduction of graphs and photographs, and so on. In some products you in fact can go considerably above the 50 per cent recycled fibre capacity for paper and still have good reproduction quality.
Then you ask what are the environmental costs of landfills and so on. For paper packaging and paper waste and so on it is now approaching one-half the contents of the dumps. In Ontario alone landfills are now consuming one and a half acres a day. One has to ask what are the costs of, rather than recycling that kind of material, putting it into dumps that produce methane and other serious problems for the environment.
Take these and other factors such as the real cost of harvesting forests which must now include the loss of fish, bird and wildlife habitat, soil erosion and the forest's role. One of the fundamentally most important matters that the Standing Committee on the Environment is now looking into is the capacity of various species of trees and plants to act as a carbon sink to take that carbon dioxide out of the atmosphere and hold it so that we do not face the horrendous consequences of global warming.
Then you plug in the green tax system which is really a very simple tax system, Mr. Speaker, as you would know. The Minister of Finance, just to deal with his day-to-day business, has dozens of feet of tax law. There are constantly new rulings. Parliament is constantly passing new laws in relation to the old tax system that we have adopted and has proven to be very negative in terms of our environment and our social development.
You plug the green tax system in at one or more levels to obtain the desired result. This is just in relation to the recycling of paper. You determine the maximum fibre
use and the minimum environmental damage and then you regulate the green tax based on your desired result.
There are amazing side benefits. The energy saving in recycled paper alone is up to 40 per cent and there is reduced marine pollution from pulp mills. We know that 40 per cent of the marine pollution of both fresh water and salt water in Canada, comes from pulp mills. You get improved air quality and improved water quality by having fewer dioxins, furons and organochlorines placed into the environment.
The staggering fact is that recycled paper is already cost competitive but because of present structures in Canadian society, including tax, marketing and industrial, it is not fully available and in fact is not available at all to many institutions such as Parliament itself.
Green taxes are not new. We have had them to encourage recycling here in Canada on glass milk bottles, for example, going back one-third of a century through the form of deposits on bottles so that people would not throw them away but would in fact send them back to the milk company to be refilled. Aluminum, steel, old batteries, beer bottles, pop bottles and many other items have been collected for the purpose of recycling.
For waste reduction the idea is catching on, from simple things such as a toilet dam which costs about $2. A toilet dam goes in the back edges of the toilet tank and reduces the amount of water that is required per flush. It might sound like a foolish thing to be raising in the opening speech on a debate on a green tax system, but simple, available Canadian-made technologies would save Canadian consumers $250 million a year on water bills. The way that you implement those kinds of measures is through a green tax system.
On packaging, many products have three or more forms of packaging. There is plastic covering on whatever you are getting, then there is another kind of styrofoam or fill, then there is a cardboard box and in many cases there are additional forms of packaging.
The green tax system would tax the waste packaging based on real energy costs and real landfill costs and designers will soon help Canadian society in phasing out the waste through the implementation of green taxes on those forms of waste.

Let us take a look at acid rain, an area where green taxes would be far more efficient and far more effective than the kinds of reduction programs that have been implemented here or are proposed to be implemented, for example, in the United States. Parliament and government can design targets in terms of tonnage and timetables in terms of the time frame for the reductions and set caps or limits so that there is not future growth of acid generation of the atmosphere.
You base those on what the environment can safely handle and you tax directly through a green tax system every gram of S02 or N02 or SOX and NOX as they are more commonly known, based on known impacts. We know that a most conservative estimate that we deal with here in Canada is that the negative impact of acid precipitation on our environment is $1 billion per year made up of several hundred million dollars in lost forest growth, the killing off of more than 15,000 lakes, the impact on human health and so on.
If one wanted to look at the calculations that have been recently done in the United States on a per annum cost to the environment, it is $7 billion per year in building and monument destruction, $16 billion per year in lung damage according to the American Lung Association, $40 billion per year in damage resulting in medical costs and lost time to workers due air pollution and $5 billion a year in loss of lakes and forest productivity in the United States.
As we learned on a visit last week to Washington, D.C. to encourage our colleagues south of the border to do something serious about acid precipitation, a 50 per cent reduction of acid precipitation production in the United States will cost only $15 billion, less than one quarter of the cost in one year of airborne pollution and acid precipitation on the U.S. public.
This green tax system will fire up the research and development arms across Canada and bring about the production of energy efficient products, energy conservation and new clean sustainable technologies. We already know that we can save 52 per cent of the energy now consumed in Canada through conservation, releasing this energy for commercial, residential and other purposes.
What about a carbon tax, something that has rarely if ever been seriously debated on the floor of this Chamber. We already know that carbon dioxide, methane, CFCs and other greenhouse gases pose a relentless

threat to the survival of planet earth. Entire countries will disappear beneath the oceans if we wait.
There are already alternatives. Mercedes Benz, for example, has produced a commercial test vehicle powered by hydrogen. One of my constituents in Prince Rupert makes his own hydrogen in his back yard out of simple wind technology through direct current, simply cracking the hydrogen from the water. He recompresses it with scuba equipment and puts it into retired aircraft oxygen cylinders. He has produced his own carburation system and has simply converted existing available North American and Japanese produced vehicles directly to hydrogen and, in fact, can operate them with the same carburation system on either gasoline or hydrogen should he want to take a long trip.
Present vehicles and future vehicles can be economically converted. A green tax on carbon is the carburetor for conversion costs because, as we know if one looks even at the more recent fossil fuel projects that are being proposed, whether it is Oslo, Lloydminster or Hibernia, those projects, at least according to their proponents, will only proceed if the Canadian taxpayers provide billions of dollars in direct welfare to those projects so that they can proceed.
It makes much more sense in the energy sector to have a green tax system in place providing for conversion to available technologies and alternatives that are more environmentally benign or, in fact, to options such as hydrogen which do not produce greenhouse gases.
The fossil fuel industry has become a leading danger to planetary survival.
Global warming is real and there is no known means to dramatically reduce C02 from fossil fuel use. We must go to alternatives.
This government has promised to reduce carbon dioxide output by 20 per cent by the year 2005 and yet has not taken any steps to substantially reduce it since the announcement was made 18 months ago. The rate is too slow and a carbon tax can make a much larger transition possible by the year 2000.
There are holes in the ozone. According to the most recent reports from Scott Base in Antarctica and from our own measurements, they are growing very fast. CFCs, or fluorocarbons as they are called, is the basic element in the cooling systems of automobiles, air conditioners in homes and businesses, refrigerators and freezers. It is frequently if not always released when the air conditioner, freezer and refrigeration units are taken to dumps. The CFCs are continuing to release unhin-

dered into the atmosphere. CFCs are still being sold in the Canadian market at basically the same price as they were before the Government of Canada announced the intention to phase out 85 per cent by the year 2000.
This is exactly the kind of area where there should be a green tax levy. A green tax levy would apply not only to new CFCs that are being produced but to those that are already in systems, encouraging municipalities, producers, and facilities that are involved in the re-gasing, whether it is of rail cars or of refrigeration units or whatever, to move much more quickly to new and available compounds, but also to safely remove and destroy those CFCs that pose one of the most severe environmental threats that we face.
A green tax will do all this by making the product as expensive as necessary for its complete and urgent removal and replacement. In all of these cases, part of the green tax can be diverted as direct funding for R and D, replacement products, retooling and refitting, or for a reverse green tax credit for environmentally friendly or benign products.
We are on the brink of disaster or to a new and exciting frontier of ecological sustainability. A GTS, a green tax system, can provide many acceptable economic and environmental impacts. It can encourage transitions from non-renewable to renewable energy. It can discourage waste in terms of packaging, reusable products and resources. It will promote recycling of paper, metals and containers. It will encourage new technologies, conservation, solar and energy efficiency. It will create new jobs. While it would require three, four or five jobs per unit, rather than one or two, in the forest sector, only a green tax can seriously address those kinds of broad resource and economic questions.
Forty thousand children will die today around the world from diseases, starvation and poor quality water. Several species will become extinct while we have this debate today. The tax system as we know it in Canada is inequitable, regressive and designed to keep afloat economic systems that are drifting us toward unparalleled disaster. A green tax system that is designed to halt the flow of persistent, toxic and bioaccumulative wastes
into our environment, that is designed to minimize energy use and resource waste, that is designed for full employment, sustainable development, proactive as well as reactive health care, sustainable agriculture, fisheries and conservation areas, preservation of existing species and recovery of our much harmed environment is the politics of Canada's future and the fate of the earth.
We must have a green tax system, not a GST or any other proposal presently being promoted by the present government and Minister of Finance.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the presentation by the hon. member for Skeena. I must say that I was moved by his futuristic concepts and the fact that he has presented before us some very creative, thought-provoking ideas in terms of our tax system.
I suppose we could raise all sorts of points, but I would like to ask my hon. colleague from Skeena a question. He is aware of organizations that have put together ethical mutual funds, funds that are raised by those people who want to invest in economic activities that have ethical implications of a very positive nature.
Does my hon. colleague foresee tax incentives that might be provided for those people who would invest in ecologically positive enterprises? Does he foresee the possibility of a youth ecological corps in which young people could be mobilized to play their role in combating environmental deterioration? Does he foresee something of the nature of an ecological mutual fund where tax incentives could be provided for those investors who would put capital aside to mobilize and fight pollution?

Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for the question. First, on the concept of ethical mutual funds, there is no doubt that they are catching the interest of a lot of Canadians who have either a small or a large amount of money that they want to invest. The ethical mutual funds look at not only the impact of a particular industry or a particular proposal on the environment, but at what kinds of plant facilities there are, what kind of collective agreements there are for the workforce and so on. They are gaining wide support from a broadening section of Canadian society.
October 31, 1989

In terms of the member's question in relation to tax incentives for those who are participating, that would not be the best approach. The best approach in fact is to apply the green tax system in relation to the resource sectors and in relation to industries themselves because the principle that is involved in ecologically sound taxation policies is to make sure that certain principles are adhered to; minimizing the amount of energy used, minimizing the amount of waste that is produced from any particular product, applying certain sound internationally respected principles such as using closed circuit technologies to make sure that persistent, toxic and bioaccumulative materials do not continue to go on to the land, into the marine environment or into the atmosphere.
The principal intention of a green tax system is and should be implemented by the Government of Canada in order to reduce waste and to move our technologies to the cutting edge. I think many of the stocks, shares and so on that would be found within an ethically sound mutual fund would be of those technologies, industries and social developments that are on the cutting edge and have been encouraged to do so by a green tax system.
The reason we do not have more accessibility and availability of renewable energy sources in this country is that it is not encouraged by the present tax system. The government has not only closed down access to public information in relation to the renewable sector, but in fact funding for R and D and so on has also been cut off. That is direct discouragement. On the other hand there is direct encouragement, through the funding of billions of dollars from Canadian taxpayers, to the nuclear and fossil fuel sectors which are now being demonstrated to be the least beneficial option either in terms of cost or energy efficiency.
The member's point on a green crop, I suppose you might call it, is one that I think Canada must look at with a much greater vigour because there are things in every single province and in both territories that require the serious address of not only young people, but society as a whole. It is often best to involve young people, either at the high school age or in the years immediately following high school, whether in terms of replanting stream banks to improve fisheries habitat or simply planting different species of trees.

There should be scientific people along who talk not only about the commercial nature of the various species that are being planted, but the benefits to fish, birds and to wildlife and also the growing threat to the planet in terms of global warming and the greenhouse effect. The process of simply replanting trees is helping to get a larger carbon sink growing that takes more of that out of the atmosphere.
In terms of ecological mutual funds, I think there is a direct relation to a green tax system in that a green tax system is ethically appropriate.
I think one of the most repugnant self-admissions by our present Minister of Finance is that he has admitted that the GST, whether it is 5 per cent or 9 per cent, is a regressive form of taxation. Why, at this point, would we be making some of the more ecologically expensive and devastating industries in terms of the long term for future generations more expensive and less likely to be able to redesign, retool and refit to make themselves, at the very least, ecologically and environmentally benign?
I think there is a great parallel between ethical mutual funds and the ethics that one finds in the kind of taxation I am talking about in terms of a green tax system.

the GST. Since that is contradictory, would the member suggest that we should ignore all those coupons coming from McDonald's opposing the GST?

Mr. Speaker, first on the member's attempt to correct the record, the Minister of Finance has stated, not only here but outside of this Chamber, that the GST is a regressive tax. It is obvious that it is a regressive tax. Any economist anywhere in the country would point out that it is a regressive tax.
On the matter of McDonald's, I do not think there would be any better or more efficient way of getting McDonald's to clean up its act than applying a green tax system to it. You would simply continue to push on the accelerator in terms of a green tax in relation to the amount of packaging they use until they go to recyclable, reusable or at least reduced packaging systems.
As the member quite properly points out, the problems that are being faced globally now as a result of the burning of the rain forests in Brazil to provide very short-term pasturage for beef in Brazil is creating a colossal problem for one of the largest parts of our global lungs.
In terms of McDonald's sending in coupons and opposing the GST, I think they are responding quite properly on behalf of their consumers. It is a bad tax and it should go.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Questions and comments are now terminated. I would like to listen to the hon. members all afternoon, but there are other members who want to speak.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak to the motion before the House today.

This motion relates to a new and insidious reality that has dramatically confronted not only Canadians but all citizens of our planet in recent times, namely that our environment is being threatened by the scourge of pollution and other ecological ills.

The problem is a global problem and requires global solutions. However, I think we can take some comfort
from the fact that more and more countries are realizing they will have to take steps to protect the environment.

Let us be clear; safeguarding the environment is one of this government's highest priorities. We are committed to positive steps that will halt the abuse of the environment and preserve this most precious natural heritage.
I do not take issue with the broad concern for the environment that is implicit in the motion. But the proposal outlined in the motion-specifically that the government implement an ecological sound green tax system-puts the cart before the horse in my view. It fails to recognize that one can only build from a sound base.
A tax system can be used to pursue good, desirable and important objectives, but only if it first meets the fundamental objectives of a tax system, namely, to provide a stable, reliable source of public revenue. This is necessary to provide Canadians with the services they need and to support an efficient and competitive economy. It is to provide Canada with just such a tax system that the government has undertaken its proposal for tax reform.
A sound, basic tax system is a key requirement for Canada's continued economic prosperity. Our objective as a government has been to ensure that Canada has a tax system that is as fair and as efficient as possible.
We have been working to achieve exactly that. In stage one of tax reform we restored fairness and efficiency to the personal and corporate tax systems. We lowered tax rates and broadened the tax base, eliminating many of the special tax breaks that distorted investment and hindered the development of an efficient, competitive economy.
Our tax reform package ensures that investment decisions are based on economic merit rather than tax considerations. It assures that corporations and higher income Canadians pay their fair share of taxes. It ensures more equitable treatment of individuals in similar economic circumstances. It ensures that Canadians in lower income brackets have a smaller tax burden in proportion to their income than higher income Canadians.
October 31, 1989

In stage two of the tax reform we are proposing to replace the existing, outdated federal sales tax with the goods and services tax.

The GST will achieve three major objectives: First, it will help the general effort to reduce the deficit and ensure that we can continue to afford the programs and services valued by Canadians. Second, it will help ensure that Canada is able to compete effectively on world markets. Finally, it will improve the basic fairness of our tax system. In fact, low and middle income Canadians will be protected when the GST is implemented.

Building a sound tax system is part of our overall strategy for ensuring a stronger, more competitive economy. During the last five years we have made considerable progress in implementing that strategy.

One of the main objectives of this plan is to deal with the need to cut back public spending, reduce our annual deficit and control the growth of the public debt. Mr. Speaker, we have made considerable progress towards achieving that objective. We have reduced spending on government operations as well as the rate of growth of program spending. Last year, we spent $1.7 billion less on government operations than in 1984-85, a drop of 10 per cent. As a result of the measures taken by the government, we were able to reduce program spending as a percentage of our gross domestic product from 19.5 per cent in 1984-85 to 16.5 per cent last year.
We have also cut the government's deficit by more than $9.5 billion compared to what it was in 1984, and we have reduced the growth of the public debt. During the past fiscal year, for the first time in 15 years the increase in the debt was below 10 per cent, compared to a peak of 24 per cent in 1984.
In addition to controlling costs, major steps have been taken to ensure that Canadians are competitive. These measures include deregulation of the energy and transportation sectors, improved training programs, a new competition policy and, of course, the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement.
Supply
These changes have helped to provide for a healthy and confident public sector. About 209,000 jobs have been created in Canada since January 1 this year, when the Free Trade Agreement came into force. These jobs are part of the 1.5 million new jobs created in Canada during the past five years.

In working to build a healthy economy this government recognizes that it is increasingly important to ensure that economic growth is compatible with the protection of our environment. The government is firmly committed to the principle that a healthy environment and a healthy economy go hand in hand. It is impossible to have one without the other.
We are giving concrete expression to this commitment by our support for the concept of sustainable development, in the policies we are pursuing here at home, as well as in initiatives we are undertaking internationally.

The public demands that we strike a new balance between the way we do business and the way we manage our environment. For governments, this means making environmental concerns a priority in economic policy development. Industry must make better use of natural resources. Our natural resources are a basic raw material for the production process and are vital to our growth and economic well-being. Our natural resources are also directly affected by production processes and the resulting waste. Finally, the general public must change its demand for consumer goods, its methods of waste disposal and indeed its way of life.
We have already seen the beginnings of a commitment to this: industries are developing codes of good environmental practice, consumers are taking part in waste recycling programs and choosing environmentally friendly products, governments are setting stricter standards to protect the environment and international agencies are developing protocols to protect the planet.
To protect our natural resources from environmental deterioration and misuse, we must ensure that consumers and producers bear the real costs of their decisions- not only the direct costs, but also all the social costs. Market forces can be channeled by creating economic incentives and deterrents that will encourage consumers, businesses and also governments to make decisions every

October 31, 1989
Supply
day for more a cost-effective resource allocation and better environmental protection.
Incentives based on market forces provide real benefits for the environment and the economy, they promote more enlightened use of natural resources, they encourage businesses to be creative in finding economic solutions and they complement the policy framework already in place.

Like most countries, historically Canada has relied mainly on regulatory approaches to protecting the environment. We continue to believe that strong regulations are necessary to deal with the variety of threats to the environment such as dangerous chemicals. Nevertheless, in other areas there is significant potential to mobilize market forces to preserve the environment and to ensure that consumers and producers of polluting products bear the environmental costs of their actions.

Many activities that are a threat to the environment are not the result of efficient markets but rather of market failures. These activities often lead to what economists call externalities, where the environmental costs of manufacturing certain products are not borne by the producer or the consumer but by society as a whole.
In fact, in the case of transboundary pollution like acid rain, the costs are borne by the citizens of other countries. Using our resources effectively, which is, after all, the key to sustainable growth, requires an accurate assessment of the real costs and benefits of production and consumption.

This is the philosophy that underlies the initiatives we have taken and that we will continue to take in the international arena to ensure that environmental protection and economic development are mutually reinforcing and not mutually exclusive. This is the approach the Prime Minister pursued with his colleagues at the Paris economic summit. It is the approach we are pursuing at the OECD, in the Commonwealth and in our proposal to
ensure that the World Bank integrates environmental concerns more effectively into its operations.
We are committed to the same principles domestically as we are internationally. We do not believe that we can rely entirely on regulatory and legal approaches. Important as they are, they essentially stop things that should not be done.

It is also important, Mr. Speaker, to encourage appropriate action, and this is where market-oriented solutions could be used, for instance by encouraging a switch to new technologies that are able to bring pollution down to levels that can be absorbed without unacceptable consequences for the environment.

The importance that this government places on the environment was made evident in the Speech from the Throne. The government identified preservation of Canada's environment as one of four fundamental objectives for this mandate.
Recent changes to the cabinet decision-making system-the creation of the cabinet committee on the environment-will ensure that all government policies and initiatives are compatible with environmental objectives.
The forming of this committee represents a major change in the governmental decision-making process. As a catalyst for this change the government has created a new institution, the National Round Table on the Environment and the Economy. The round table brings together representatives from government, business, environmental groups and the academic world to seek acceptable means of reconciling environmental concerns and economic challenges.
While round table members may have diverse views and priorities, they share a common goal: to harmonize economic and other types of development with the need to conserve the environment.

Mr. Speaker, my colleague, the Minister of the Environment, has announced that this government is preparing an exhaustive action plan that will translate the concept of sustainable development into real terms in Canada.

Although it will take many years to implement, this plan will provide a framework for initiatives that will help us change our decision-making.
Our environmental action plan will improve our decisions by providing for better scientific knowledge, and training, more reliable data, better communications and more widespread use of advanced technology to monitor and report on the state of the environment.

Our plan will emphasize the importance of maintaining partnerships and establishing new ones among all elements of society-governments, industry, labour, non-governmental agencies, citizen groups and individual Canadians.
The federal government is taking responsibility for implementing the environmental action plan. Because the market-place cannot by itself establish the proper framework for responsible decisions on environment issues, governments at all levels must establish roles governing activities that affect the environment. We must establish the value of the environment through regulations, laws, and through economic and financial penalties and rewards.
As I have suggested, selective environmentally-oriented tax measures can have a place in our tax system in cases where this is the most effective means of achieving specific goals. However, as I said at the start, a modem, efficient tax system cannot be designed to achieve one single desirable goal, no matter how desirable. We must have a fundamentally sound, fair and efficient tax system before considering the use of the tax system to pursue so profound and wide-reaching objective.

Mr. Speaker, I may recall and repeat that this government has made a commitment to take all necessary steps to protect and preserve our environment.
We encourage policies that are ecologically sound. We do not oppose them. In fact, considering the complexity and extent of the pollution problem in Canada, we must seek new and imaginative solutions.
Supply

However, the opposition motion ignores the wider range of considerations that a responsible government must take into account. Canada must first have in place a stable, reliable tax system that will ensure our economy and fiscal health. Only when such a tax system is fully in place can we be sure we will have both the means and the ability to achieve the goal this motion seeks.

That, in a few words, is what this government is doing, Mr. Speaker, and for the reasons just mentioned, I believe the House should reject this motion.

Mr. Speaker, the environment is something that concerns not only the members in this House, not only the average Canadian, but every person around the globe. We must stop borrowing the land from our children. We must work very hard to protect the environment in the future.
In the Scarborough area very close to my riding there is a committee called Save the Rouge Committee, that is working very hard. It is an area where there is talk that an expressway will go through, where houses will be built. It is an area where children at the present time go for school trips to clean up the environment, and they feel happy about it. It is an area for wildlife and where metro residents can go to enjoy themselves.
However, I heard the hon. member across the way talk about tax reform, and about the GST being 9 per cent. Clearly I was just baffled. Has the member not listened to the people of Canada, 80 per cent of whom are saying that they are opposed to the 9 per cent GST? Yesterday, outside, we had thousands of people voicing their concern against the GST.
The member rambled on about how fair the taxation is that the government is implementing and how it is working to reduce the deficit. I am just wondering if the member is in a nightmarish state and he has to open his eyes and see exactly what the people of Canada want.
Yes, the people of Canada want a better environment. However, the people of Canada have repeatedly said, "No, no, no" to the 9 per cent GST.

October 31, 1989
Supply
Just the other day my children brought home a form that I had to fill out and send to the government stating that we are against the GST because they will be taxed on their skating lessons. My little daughter asked me, "Dad, does that mean that I will have to pay more?". I am just wondering how the hon. member would answer this question to future generations of Canadians, how he will tell them that they have to pay more for their music lessons, more for their skating lessons and more for everything else. We are again turning around and taxing our education.
The Prime Minister stands up there and says, "We created 1.4 million jobs after the free trade legislation came in". These jobs are hamburger helpers at McDonald's.
My question for the minister is this. When will this government actually open its eyes and ears and see what the Canadian people want and listen to the Canadian people and stop rambling on about reducing the deficit? Since this government came into power the debt has doubled. Probably by the time the people of Canada kick you out, you will have taken it up by four times. The government should actually see what it has done to this country. It has taken it down the tubes.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to tell the hon. member that since we have come to government the deficit has not doubled. It has been lowered by approximately $10 billion, which is something important that he needs to know.
Second, when I listen to the description the hon. member from across this hall gives of our tax reform, I am not surprised that Canadians have some hesitation. But we will proceed to explain to them that this change is needed, that this change is a modem change, that it is a fair change.
I heard a little while back another hon. member say that the Minister of Finance had admitted that the GST was regressive-not at all. What the Minister of Finance has said is that sales tax can be regressive, and we have taken every measure to make sure that it is not so.
So we are talking about the deficit. We are taking the necessary measures to guarantee the income this government needs in order to provide Canadians with their programs. I can assure the hon. member that we will continue to do so.
He must agree that the decision we have taken to proceed with tax reform has not been done because we want to be popular. It has been taken because it is needed for this country. We are putting aside a tax which is devastating to our economy. We are doing it, following a model that is used in a large number of modem countries. Therefore, I do not agree with him on his conclusion.
I think that the environment, like all social programs, is threatened, not by decisions of any one government, but by the state of the finances of this country, which have to be put in order.
We inherited a very high deficit. We have worked to bring it down. It has been difficult, but we will continue to do so because we consider this to be the best way to guarantee this program, and to tackle environmental problems which are with us.

Mr. Speaker, my question for the Minister of State for Finance is in relation to the concluding remarks he made, that there needs to be some further changes to our tax system before any serious consideration can be given to bringing in environmentally appropriate taxation or a green tax system.
I would like the minister to address some of the simple points that I made when I was speaking. How does he explain that it is appropriate to tax bicycles under the GST at the same rate as motor vehicles, virgin paper at the same rate as recycled paper, and to tax a non-polluting industry producing any given product at the same rate as a similar industry that in fact is a polluting one?
If one looks at the nature of the environmental problems facing Canada, one sees that they are broad, they are severe, and they are increasing in their severity right across the country, whether it is with respect to toxic and hazardous waste or the movement of persistent and bio-accumulative materials into the Great Lakes and St. Lawrence system. What is happening is that every major run of fish in the world is on the decline, which is true of the Canadian fisheries as well. There is the rate of soil erosion to be looked at, and so on. If you talk to any economist you can find a direct link between the form of taxation that is taking place, the rate of environmental decline, and the amount of waste that is going on in our society.
October 31, 1989

The minister says that we have to wait until some future, more regressive tax measures are put in place before doing anything serious about the environment. Does the minister support the concept of a green tax system, or does he only support the kind of tax measures that are in place or being proposed by the present Minister of Finance?

Mr. Speaker, what we support are all the measures that will enable this government to assume its full responsibility in all sectors. As I have indicated, we are changing a tax system which is very porous, which threatens the resources of the government, resources which are needed.
The member talks about bicycles. It is very easy to be very emotional about any particular item which is taxed, but bicycles are already taxed. He may not know that. A lot of other things are taxed directly or indirectly.
What we have been very careful about doing is providing a very generous credit system by exempting a certain number of basic essential products so that the system is fair. Once people are given the capacity to make their own choice they are not hampered by our reform.
This tax is far from being regressive. If we start removing this or that article, you will have to increase the rate, as the hon. member obviously knows. We are getting away from a tax system in which there are 75,000 tax collectors and 22,000 different particular arrangements, which are throwing our economy into a state of disorder.
These are central issues that we have to tackle in order to face the problems, which I agree are serious. The greatest reward or the greatest hope we can have is that we, at long last, are tackling these problems of the environment which have been with us a very long time.
I am very hopeful that all together we can pull out of this very damaging situation and make sure that we pass on a better world to our children.

Mr. Speaker, to keep it short, the minister speaks about how devastating the federal sales tax has been on the economy, and his word was "devastating". I think Canadians will note that his government has increased the tax from 9 per cent to 13.5 per cent, thereby increasing the devastation by 50 per cent.
Supply
I would like to ask the minister this. Since he does not feel this tax is regressive, and since he thinks that the government has taken measures to ensure that it will not be regressive, why on earth does this government refuse to index the sales tax credit so that the poorest in our society can be assured that they are not going to be punished any more by this tax?

Mr. Speaker, we are very glad to stand by our record. We are the government that has put in place a tax credit for the sales tax. We have always been very careful to adapt it and raise it as needed in order to meet the same objective we have given, which is to have the fairest possible tax system. We will continue to do that.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with interest to the motion introduced today by the hon. member for Skeena. I salute him and congratulate him for his initiative. It is a timely initiative, drawing our attention, in the broader context of tax reform and fiscal policy, to the possibilities that the tax system can provide for better environmental control and for improved services, both municipal and federal, to the people of Canada.
Most people in Canada, of course, as in many countries, see pollution as something that directly touches their lives, a matter often closely linked with public health. The challenge facing governments is to persuade people that curbing pollution is always in their interest, and that, invariably, it costs money.
In the past, Canadian governments and, indeed, governments in many western countries, have chosen to pursue the "command" route: thou shall not pollute. More recently, a number of European countries in particular have explored the possibilities of using the tax system as a method of encouraging environmental policies.
I have in mind the fact that Sweden taxes the active ingredients in pesticides and fertilizers. Finland and Norway impose charges on non-returnable containers, Italy on plastic bags, and Sweden on batteries containing mercury or cadmium. One could continue, for the examples are many. The initiatives in Europe are certainly something that Canada could look at with benefit. I suspect that my colleague for Skeena may have had such initiatives in mind when he introduced his motion today.

October 31, 1989
Supply
Traditionally, governments have used the tax system for purposes other than merely to raise revenues. In a variety of ways and over the past century there have developed in Canada methods within the tax system either to encourage certain economic policies or to discourage certain practices considered to be contrary to the public interest.
The government-and I do not speak merely of this government but of previous governments as well-has sought in the Income Tax Act, the Excise Tax Act and the Customs Act various ways in which to encourage environmental policies, particularly in the corporate world.
In all those cases, and I could cite one or two other examples of the tax system being used as a method of encouraging better pollution control, they are only effective if they are coupled with broader governmental policy on the environment. In other words, if we are to make further use of the tax system as a method of encouraging better environmental practices, then it must be linked to the environmental laws and policies that we already have in place.
I mentioned the Income Tax Act. Capital cost allowances under the Income Ihx Act have provided for the depreciation of equipment relating to pollution control. It may be that the government would like to examine further the possibilities of accelerating the write-off of capital costs as an additional incentive to corporations, both with regard to water and air pollution.
The capital cost allowance write-off was three years. I believe that it is now two years. The government may wish to look again at that term to see whether some further incentive might be provided under accelerated capital cost allowances so that equipment would be purchased and put in place now for the future benefit of the environment and, indeed, the benefit of all Canadians.
I would also remind the House that the Income Tax Act has been used as a means of directly influencing environmental behaviour. The Oil Substitution Program were two elements of the National Energy Program that is now largely forgotten, but which did bring real benefit in terms of environmental improvement.
The Excise Ihx Act is a second example of government tax policy which can have an effect on the environment.
It provides for exemptions and reductions for a broad range of policy reasons. The government may want, as it revises and reviews the Excise Tax Act, to look again at its schedules of exempt equipment to see whether they are, indeed, comprehensive enough, whether they offer the municipalities in particular the possibilities of installing and improving the level of the equipment that they have available to them for pollution control.
Finally, of course, customs duties have also been a method whereby the import of pollution control equipment could be facilitated. Under the free trade agreement with the United States those duties will be eliminated. But, of course, the United States is not the only source of good pollution control equipment. Therefore, the government may wish to consider what further measures could be taken under the customs tariff to determine whether equipment from other than the United States might be made more readily available in Canada.
I have said that the tax measures cannot be viewed in isolation. In the case of environmental control incentives, if they are to be efficacious, the tax measures should be directly related to other programs that the government is conducting in the environmental area.
I do, however, want to say more about possibilities for the future. There has been a whole range of suggestions, and I regret to say less from this House than from outside this House, that has come forward about the use of the tax system as one route toward improved environmental control. These have ranged from additional deductions for scientific research to proposals for capital cost allowances for pollution control devices. We have seen more recently even more imaginative proposals that have been brought forward which have a direct effect on our tax system.
I speak, of course, of the idea of environmental bonds which have been advocated, I believe, by some members of this House, and certainly by a number of our fellow Canadians. Taking the United States example, a municipality floats a bond and the interest paid on that bond to the bondholder is exempt from federal taxes. That type of bond related to environmental purposes might be developed in Canada. A municipality, for environmental purposes, could introduce a bond, the interest on which would be deemed tax-free by the federal government. That is one area where some substance might be given to

the proposal of the hon. member for Skeena for a so-called green tax.
Many of us also will be aware of the initiatives taken by some Canadians to put forward the idea of environmental mutual funds. Particularly in Vancouver we have seen the initiative taken to limit the investment of certain mutual funds to those companies whose processes or products are considered environmentally respectable. The incentive for those mutual funds to invest in the companies making such products or conducting certain procedures, is limited of course by the profitability of those companies.
It may be that within the tax system there are ways in which investment in mutual funds directly related to the environment could be encouraged by a tax incentive.
The question of environmental flow-through shares has also been raised on a number of occasions, the comparison being with the flow-through shares in the oil and gas industry where basically the benefits of the profitability of the company flows directly through to the shareholder. The tax benefits normally earned by the corporation can be passed on to investors by the company renouncing its use of those benefits.
It may be that with some imagination and perseverance, it would be possible for us to develop within Canada, again basing ourselves on the precedent of the oil and gas flow-through shares, such a practice within the environmental area as well.
In conclusion, I want to say a word more about sales taxes, which of course are very much on everyone's minds these days. With regard to enviornmental incentives, the precedent in the case of the manufacturers' sales tax is there. The Minister of State for Finance will know that the present manufacturers' sales tax does provide, in a number of instances, for the exemption or reduction of the tax on products that are intended for environmental control.
I know that as soon as one puts forward the proposal for exemptions from a sales tax, one gets into a complicated area of public policy. But it may be that if the government chooses to pursue its present policy of exempting certain products and services from the effect of its proposed goods and services tax, it may want also to look again at its former practice of exempting pollution control equipment from the sales tax and consider
Supply
whether it wishes to extend that practice into the new tax.
There is another possibility, in my view, where we could seek the opportunity to use taxation as a method of encouraging better environmental practices, and that is to try to develop an emissions tax. We have effectively provided for such an emissions tax in the case of automobile gasoline. Indeed, in Europe today there is a number of countries pursuing different taxations for different types of emissions by, for example, taxing unleaded petrol at a lower rate than leaded petrol.
The case that I have in mind is whether we can use an emissions tax as an effective method of encouraging better environmental practices when related to other government initiatives in the environmental field. I believe that we could.
There are methods of establishing environmental norms against which the practices of any corporation could be measured, whether it be in the area of air or water emissions, and a tax levied for those who are not meeting the norm. I want to acknowledge at once that a tax is paid only by a profitable company. In a number of instances the worst polluters are companies of only marginal profitability or indeed those that are not profitable at all. Therefore, broadly speaking, the effectiveness of a so-called green tax or a tax system along the lines that I imagine the hon. member from Skeena has in mind can be limited by the fact that a company must be profitable to respond to tax incentives.
I might conclude what I have offered this morning with the observation that today firms are often financially worse off by being good environmental citizens. There is not, in effect, a broadly based incentive for corporations to seek better environmental practices. I would join with our colleague from Skeena in seeking, through the tax system, any opportunity to make it profitable for companies to benefit from the introduction of better environmental controls and procedures.

In listening to the hon. member's remarks it seems that he is supportive of the idea of a green tax system. As I am sure he is aware, the present process of prosecution under the Fisheries Act for allowing persistent or biocumulative materials to go into the Great Lakes, the St. Lawrence, or into the salt water environment, simply is not working. In fact under the Canadian

Supply
Environmental Protection Act there has only been one prosecution since the act was proclaimed.
We know that prosecution is simply not working, even though we have the concept of zero discharge included in our bilateral treaty with the United States on Great Lakes Water Quality. As we learned both from the IJC and the more recent reports from both Canadian and environmental authorities, the quality of the Great Lakes is continuing to go down. We know in terms of the atmosphere that the same is true. The quality of the air in Canada is continuing to decline. Prosecution and fines are not the way to encourage industries to clean up.
I wonder if the member could spend a moment to reflect on whether or not it is appropriate to bring in something like the GST which will tax recycled paper at the same 9 per cent rate as virgin paper. That is certainly not going to encourage the more environmentally appropriate use of recycled paper. In relation to waste reduction whether it is coming from a smokestack into the atmosphere, or from a pipe into a river, lake, or the ocean, or in terms of the more than 50 per cent of hazardous and toxic waste that is being illegally and improperly disposed of across the country, the prosecution route is not working. That stick is not working.
Would the member not agree that the carrot approach of a varying green tax in relation to minimizing energy used, minimizing waste production, and moving toward the cutting edge of technologies and renewable energy, is the route we should be going with our tax policies in Canada? We know that our environment is becoming increasingly degraded. We are facing significant levels of unemployment in areas where we in fact should have full employment in the resource production areas. By adding another layer of regressive tax, it will simply accelerate the rate of environmental destruction rather than reduce it.
It seems the member is supporting the concept of a green tax, but could he clarify exactly where the Liberal party stands in relation to a green tax system and compare it to the GST as proposed by the Minister of Finance.

I certainly agree with the hon. member that the "command and control" approach to environmental matters is not often the most effective. Depending on how that approach is applied, it can penalize new entrants to an industry, since regulations are probably tougher on new entrants than they are on existing producers. Quite often the command and control procedure, for whatever reasons, is much less effective than the incentive system. I have no dispute with the member for Skeena in that regard; obviously it should be the carrot rather than the stick.
However, I want him to recognize that using the incentive system has some real problems. I was not certain this morning whether in his discussion he would become specific about what particular fiscal measures he envisaged to give substance to his green tax idea.
Having said that, let me add that in the case of the Liberal party-and I did not wish to interject any particular partisan note into this question because I think it is one question that concerns us all, I recall that it was a Liberal government of the late 1970s and through the early 1980s which did introduce various fiscal measures intended to provide incentives for corporations to introduce procedures environmentally improved over what they had been before. The record of the Liberal governments, while perhaps not always as aggressive or as imaginative as one might wish, did at least point in the right direction.
In the case of the manufacturers' sales tax, which was then 9 per cent and subsequently 11 per cent, the Liberal government of the day did provide exemptions for improved pollution control equipment.
Now we have the government of the day offering a goods and services tax which to my knowledge, except possibly in the case of municipal taxation, does not offer any comparable incentives for environmental improvement. It is for the government, in deciding whether it will set the rate of tax at 9 per cent or 7 per cent, whether it will also offer rebates for the equipment for improved environmental control. That is an option open to the government. I have not yet heard this government come forward with such exemptions or rebates. It may be that the Minister of State for Finance, if he were with us, would want to respond to the question of how indeed the

federal government intends to tax under the GST the services and the equipment used by municipalities, many of which are directly concerned with environmental control.
I for one share with the member for Skeena some puzzlement by what the government intends to do with regard to the imposition of the goods and services tax on municipalities. If we could at least have such clarification today, that alone would justify the member's motion.

Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate my colleague from Etobicoke North for what I thought was the very clear and scientific way in which he developed his position.
I just want to go back to the comments of the previous speaker from the other side of the House and try my colleague from Etobicoke North on a concern which I have and which I think all Canadians have. They set out something that was an action plan and it contained four vital elements. One of them in the future would have a great concern for the environment.
In other words, I think what they meant was that things would be put to the test and, if they could not stand the test in relation to what this action would do to the environment, they would not allow it; they would condemn it.
I am really puzzled as to why they would take the action that they have in reference then to VIA. Rail transportation has been proven to be the most compatible with the environment as far as emissions standards and the like. I am not aware of any public input that was allowed or any study that was done and released to the public to show that there was any concern there at all.
In your opinion do you think that they have broken with what they set out as a very noble set of conditions? And I think Canada would applaud those, however at almost the first opportunity that comes along, deliberately or otherwise-presumably an ignorance of their own rules-they put this out to the Canadian people without any discussion or any seeming justification for it. Certainly it has not been proven to be the most accepted way to go as far as environment is concerned in reference to mass transportation.
Would my colleague from Etobicoke North comment?
Supply

The hon. member is of course quite right. In its decisions with respect to VIA the government has not limited itself by environmental considerations. Equally in its policy of airport expansion and, as the hon. member has put it, in mass transport generally we see no real commitment on the part of the government to take into account environmental considerations before making its final decisions with regard to the abolition of rail services or the expansion of airports. Both of those policies have major environmental considerations. It is a deplorable fact that this government has not seen fit to consider the environmental elements before announcing its commitment to the expansion of airports and the reduction of rail services.
With regard to rail services in particular, it seems to me self-evident that with the investment of additional funds in rail services not only would the services be improved for certain communities but, broadly speaking, the environmental impact would be a positive one.
In the name of deficit reduction, which is an understandable policy on the part of the government, it has decided to reduce those services, to reduce those government expenditures. It has not, however, shown any inclination to tackle the real problem which is high interest rates which make the deficit so high and which in turn encourages the government to turn to such alternatives in its view as reducing rail services or other environmentally damaging practices. I agree with the hon. member that the government has acted hastily and acted with only short-term considerations in mind.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I regret that the time for questions and comments has now terminated. The hon. member for Yorkton-Melville.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in a debate which is a very important one in terms of a new idea for our tax system that has not been pursued in this country before. It is the fact that we have a tax system that takes into account the ecology. The motion of the hon. member for Skeena reads as follows:
That this House calls upon the government to implement an
ecologically sound "green" tax system.

October 31, 1989
Supply
I believe, as most people around the world believe, that we do not have too much time left in terms of saving the planet from the pollutants that we are constantly spewing out into the water, the atmosphere, our food system, and into the earth. We have to do whatever we can in this country and around the world to tiy to reverse the very dangerous direction that this world is going in.
Our country, despite its small population, despite its relative economic wealth, abundance of resources and progressivity in terms of social and economic programs, is one of the worst pollutants on a per capita basis in the world. I think that is a very sad commentary of where we have been and where we are as a country.
The question we must ask ourselves is: How can we change that? I think the member for Skeena has made a recommendation today that is very important about how we can go a major distance into changing how we look at our environment and what we do to the environment. If you look at the history in our country and other countries around the world, we find that tax policy has a tremendous impact on the social and economic policies and institutions of this country and other countries around the world.
We see around the world example after example of governments reaching out for their objectives through the taxation system and making sure that certain things happen because of a taxation system in this world and in this country in particular.
We see in the provinces as well social economic policy being determined in part by taxation policy. I know that in my own province of Saskatchewan, which is very rural, we often have taxation regimes that help people living in rural communities, small towns, farms, communities that are a long way from the major cities of Regina and Saskatoon. I suggest that we can do the same thing with the taxation system here.
I want to make the assertion-and I hope you agree, Mr. Speaker-that our present taxation system is one that was designed for the horse and buggy in terms of the modern problems of the environment. It is antiquated, out of date, and out of touch in terms of doing something real about the environmental problems that we have.
I will give a few examples of what I mean. The government across the way has introduced a goods and
services tax. It is a 9 per cent tax across the board touching everything from the pizza that you are going to buy, Mr. Speaker, to the haircut you will have every once in a while, to what goes into the inputs of industry, and so on. It is a tax that covers a broad sweep, regardless of whether or not that industry or that activity is polluting the atmosphere. It does not discriminate in favour of companies, activities, or products that help keep this planet green. It does not discriminate against companies, products, or activities that indeed pollute the environment and make this world a much worse place in which to live.
It is an antiquated system. It is a system that has to be changed. For example, the goods and services tax will have the same tax on a bicycle as on a motorcycle. A motorcycle will pollute the atmosphere where a bicycle will not. It will have the same tax on cycled paper as on recycled paper. Recycled paper in the first place costs more than virgin paper, yet the tax is the same. It will have the same kind of tax on alternative forms of energy as on energy that is based on fossil fuel. It will have the same kind of tax on motor boats as canoes. Yet of course a motor boat will pollute the atmosphere and the waterways a lot more obviously than one without a motor.
We will have a tax that will not discriminate at all on the basis of whether or not a contribution is made to keep our planet green, beautiful, and alive for this generation and future generations.
Perhaps what Parliament should do is to take this motion put before the House today by the hon. member for Skeena and in a very non-partisan way refer the idea to a parliamentary committee or to a task force for a thorough study of how we can change the taxation system in this country to make sure that it helps produce at the end of the road a planet that is liveable, safe, decent, and clean for this generation and generations that are to come. That would be a very useful activity of a number of members of Parliament in terms of a contribution to the economy and a contribution to the environment in the years that lie ahead. I think that that is something that could be done.
I believe that taxes in this country should reflect the cost of a product to the environment. The current taxation system does not reflect that at all.
October 31, 1989

I remember back in 1969, Mr. Speaker, about a year after the two of us were elected, when the then Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau brought in a novel idea. It was called the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. It was to set aside some moneys for places like the Atlantic provinces, the Gaspe, northern Quebec, northern Ontario, and parts of western Canada to try to stimulate growth in the areas that were slower growing in this country. It was an area to use fiscal policy in order to provide economic development for people in this country who lived in areas where the market forces were not useful in terms of producing jobs.
I think now, some 20 years later, the time has come to change the taxation system in this country where one of the prime motivators is going to be the impact in terms of greening this country and greening the planet, along with other prime principles like progressivity and the ability to pay for ordinary Canadians.
That is perhaps a very radical idea. It is a very radical idea, but I think it is an idea whose time has come. The time has come to make sure we penalize companies that pollute, that we penalize individuals that pollute. A simple way of doing that is through the taxation system. It is a way that is not complicated, and it is not bureaucratic. It is a way that can be done that is in tune with the tradition of our times. It is something that can be done that is very, very useful. I think that that green tax system should reflect the environmental cost of manufacturing products in this country. I think that the money that we receive from that system can be churned over once again into promoting a greener planet and a greener Canada.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
