Mr. Speaker, for the first time in Canada, 1,100 parole officers of the federal correctional service will go on strike next Monday morning, unless an immediate agreement is reached between the Canadian Union of Public Employees and Treasury Board. These public servants have not had a salary increase since December 1986 and have to work in deteriorating conditions. Mr. Speaker, if Treasury Board does not take these workers' demands more seriously, maybe it will take the security of Canadians more seriously, because if these 1,100 parole officers decide to walk out at the same time, who will supervise and monitor all the paroled prisoners?
It is imperative that the government act this week to keep this situation from worsening and all labour relations in the Public Service from deteriorating as a result.

Mr. Speaker, representatives of the major fisheries unions in Canada are meeting here today in Ottawa to discuss the growing crisis in their industry.
A serious question has arisen. Who in this government is responsible for fisheries policy? Legislation before the U.S. Congress threatens the Canadian lobster industry. It calls for a ban on the import of lobster under a certain size. The Minister for International Trade describes these efforts as trade protectionism at its rankest. The Prime Minister told the House that the full weight and influence of the Canadian government will be brought to bear on behalf of Canadian fishermen.
What of our Minister of Fisheries? His briefing book prepared for the media reassures us that the new regulations are being brought forward for conservation reasons. Why has the minister judged the U.S. claim so favourably, thus prejudicing any case this country may make in terms of protecting our crucial market? Could the Minister of Fisheries explain why U.S. claims of

October 31, 1989
conservation are legitimate when his fellow cabinet minister and the Prime Minister so obviously disagree?

Mr. Speaker, I rise to draw to your attention today the presence in Ottawa of a group of Canada's leading performing artists, some of whom are with us here and who have come to promote the issue of performers rights in the context of the second phase of amendments to the Copyright Act.
For the benefit of those who will be unable to meet with these performers today, members of this Elouse should be aware that these performers are seeking the right to be compensated for the use of their performances.
This government is very sensitive to these concerns, and will be taking them into consideration in planning the final phase of copyright revision. Moreover, the government is committed to broader initiatives that will enhance the socio-economic status of our artists and the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture will begin reviewing this important subject next week.

Mr. Speaker, just a few hundred metres from this spot, one of Canada's most beautiful and historically important rivers, the Rideau, enters the Ottawa at the Rideau Falls.
This river makes its way slowly through the national capital and contributes much to the beauty of Ottawa and the pride that most Canadians have in their capital city, surely one of the most beautiful in the world.
But tragically, Mr. Speaker, the Rideau has become a symbol of what has gone wrong in Canada. Its waters are polluted, its beaches are closed, and no one that I know would think of eating a fish drawn from the lower Rideau.
The problems of the Rideau do not exist in isolation. They reflect the strains on water systems throughout Canada. But surely the Rideau should be a symbol of what is right in Canada. This historic waterway, flowing through the heart of our capital, is a challenge to
governments at all levels to prove our commitment to a clean and healthy environment.
That is why over 1,500 residents of Ottawa South in petition have urged the Government of Canada to engage in co-operation with the provincial and local levels of government to demonstrate on the Rideau a model of river clean-up and maintenance. I ask, Mr. Speaker, if the Rideau cannot be made clean, how can there be hope for the major industrial waterways of our country?

Mr. Speaker, health care for residents of northern Quebec is a major problem because hospitals providing a full range of basic services are rare in Matagami, Joutel, Lebel-sur-Quevillon, Desmaraisville, Miquelon and Waswanipi. Furthermore, many communities in northern Canada face a chronic shortage of physicians and hospital staff, which forces residents of these towns and villages to go to urban centres at great expense.
The task force on financial compensation for isolated northern communities wants to abolish travel deductions paid by the employer for medical reasons and also the deductions for two vacation trips a year.
Mr. Speaker, if Canada cannot afford to allow northern Canadians to travel for medical reasons, why does our government not reduce the size of ministerial delegations and abolish publicly funded travel abroad for members of Parliament who are part of a parliamentary association or Commons committee?

Mr. Speaker, I was honoured this past Friday to present on behalf of the Minister for International Trade the Canada Export Award to Connors Brothers. Located in my riding of Carleton-Charlotte Connors Brothers is the largest sardine processing plant in North America employing close to 3,500 people, and exports its canned herring, sardines, and kippers to over 30 countries

around the world. In fact, exports account for 70 per cent of its production.
In addition to maintaining its strong market share of the United States, Australia, New Zealand, and the Caribbean, Connors Brothers this past year entered new markets in Israel, Mexico, the Philippines, Bolivia, and Hong Kong.
Since the Canada Exports Program was initiated in 1983 only 95 companies have been recognized for their contributions to the expansion of Canada's export capabilities.
Connors Brothers stands as an example that given the opportunity, Canadian businesses in every region of the country can successfully compete in the increasingly competitive global market-place.

Mr. Speaker, the task force report on tax benefits for northerners and isolated areas calls for one northern zone, thereby eliminating many hundreds of communities across Canada from the current northern residents deduction.
In Kenora-Rainy River some 35 communities will lose the benefit if the government accepts the recommendation of the task force. If the recommendation of a single northern zone is accepted, employers will be faced with a dwindling workforce as workers leave northern Ontario and head south where the cost of living is cheaper.
The Dona Lake gold mine in Pickle Lake is already suffering from a shortage of workers and without the northern residents deduction it will have a more difficult time of it.

The Government must remember that the main purpose of this program was to encourage workers to go north where there are jobs.

If the government fails to keep this in mind hundreds of jobs will be lost to the south. I urge the government and the Minister of Finance to ignore the one-zone concept included in the report and to come up with
multiple zones and graduated levels of benefits which are equitable and simple.

Mr. Speaker, last week the Canadian Centre for Arms Control and Disarmament issued a significant report on Arctic arms control and security co-operation. This report was in response to proposals on Arctic security made by Soviet General Secretary Gorbachev in October, 1987. Unfortunately, the Canadian government's response to the Arctic arms control proposals by Gorbachev has been negative.
Is it not time that this government adopt a new attitude to arms control, particularly with the Arctic? Unless we start playing an active role, Canada runs the risk of allowing arms control to be bypassed in the thawing of east-west relations. The Prime Minister will have a golden opportunity to help make Arctic security co-operation a realizable goal when he visits with Gorbachev next month. While Arctic security is not on the formal agenda, the Prime Minister can further the cause by initiating some informal discussions. At a minimum, the government should accept two of the Arms Control Centre's recommendations. It should create an ambassador for circumpolar affairs, and it should extend the open-sky proposals to include the Arctic Ocean region.
There are historic opportunities to dismantle the military apparatus that has been built up during the cold war. I urge this government to take a leadership role in bringing about a secure and demilitarized north.

Mr. Speaker, as you well know, Canada is a trading nation. Our exports around the globe support three million Canadian jobs. By supporting the free trade agreement Canadians showed they understand the importance of competing internationally and expanding our export sector. That is why I am proud to rise here today to congratulate Westcan Alfalfa Inc. of Regina on winning the 1989 Canada Export Award.
Westcan is an excellent example of the progressive entrepreneurial spirit found in Regina and throughout Saskatchewan. The determination and initiative shown by Westcan Alfalfa is what will be needed to drive the Canadian economy forward in the face of tough interna-

October 31, 1989
tional competition. It is a good example to those who would have Canadians believe that we cannot compete with the rest of the world.
I know that the leadership shown Westcan Alfalfa will encourage other Regina companies to enter the international marketplace and bring increased prosperity to Saskatchewan and Canada.

The Minister of Fisheries has been hiding behind a report of the Scotia-Fundy Industry Capacity Advisory Committee. He has used this report as his bible to give direction to a hard-pressed inshore fishery in the Scotia-Fundy region.
The members of that committee acted in good faith, something I am beginning to realize this minister knows nothing about. At no time did the committee feel that this report would be acted upon in isolation. One has only to look at the report to know that it could not be taken in isolation from the problems in the groundfish management plan and the offshore fleet capacity. The first page of the report states: "The committee emphasizes that quantification of over-capacity of any fleet sector is a direct function of the resource allocations available to that sector. Thus, implementation of capacity reduction programs should be preceded by resolution of long-term resource shares. Although the review of this offshore enterprise allocation program was undertaken by DFO while this committee was functioning, the committee could not achieve success of what it viewed as the important results of that review" without review of the offshore program.
As well, the last sentence of this report, and there are only 11 pages, states that: "The committee now seeks a commitment from DFO to complete the task, in continued consultation with industry". I say, Mr. Speaker, that at no time did the members of the committee see this report implemented before a further in-depth study of the critical areas be done. This has not been done, it is not being done.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday's noon-hour incident was indeed unfortunate even more so unnecessary and uncalled for. Arrangements had been made prior to the demonstration which would have permitted an agreed on number of cabs to drive by the Centre Block in a safe and orderly fashion. However, once it became apparent these conditions were being changed, the RCMP responded in an appropriate and responsible manner. An earlier 12-minute fire alarm only enhanced the fundamental need for access to the Centre Block.
Less appropriate were the actions of some members opposite. Certainly in a democracy the people have an inalienable right to demonstrate and express their opinions. This, however, must be done in a safe and responsible manner. As such, the choice of some colleagues opposite to aid and abet a demonstration which clearly would raise security concerns and deny emergency access to the House of Commons borders on irresponsibility. It is incumbent upon us as Members of Parliament to fully recognize a proper and important role which security and safety assumes in this place for all members, their staff and the staff of House of Commons. In the future, let us all work together to continue to make this place an accessible, secure and safe place for us all, not simply for a select few.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on the same subject as my colleague. To demonstrate publicly and legally in support of or against an issue is one of our basic rights as citizens.
Yesterday's efforts by cab drivers and others to focus attention on the goods and services tax was no exception. In the course of those events, officers of the RCMP had difficulty in meeting their obligation to ensure access to Parliament Hill for emergency service and for those people, including MPs and Senators, who work here. I hope that all in this place, government supporters and opposition alike, will act to uphold the RCMP when officers act to protect the persons and property that comprise the Parliament of Canada. It was disheartening to witness on the TV reports of the incident yesterday the intolerance of some of the demonstrators in their
October 31, 1989

attack on the young man who publicly supports the GST as the best alternative to the unfair and long out of date sales tax on Canadian manufacturers.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Secretary of State for External Affairs said in response to my leader's question about Canada's ability to act independently within the OAS: "We set Canadian policy here in Canada for Canadian reasons. That is our practice, that will continue to be our practice".
Will the Secretary of State practice what he preached? Will Canada denounce continued covert aid to the Contras whose present activities have resulted in the death of hundreds and which threaten to destabilize Nicaraguan peace process? Will Canada denounce the $9 million spent by the United States government in support of opposition parties in the Nicaraguan election as an unacceptable intrusion in the internal affairs of another state?
In short, will Canada resist the OAS' historic compliance with U.S. military and political intervention in the affairs of member states, or will the Secretary of State be fearful that in reflecting Canadian opinion the Americans will perceive him, as they did Douglas Roche, as too vigorous?

Mr. Speaker, Canadian performers are in Ottawa today with flowers and with the message that bouquets are not enough. Performers are playing a primary role in the shaping and strengthening of our Canadian cultural identity, our national consciousness. Accolades are fine, but it will not put food on creators tables, it will not look after their social benefits or their tax concerns. That is not going to happen until the status of these artists is given full professional standing.
Oral Questions
My question, in the absence of the Minister of Communications, is for the Prime Minister. I want to know, artists want to know and Canadians want to know when will he introduce status of the artists legislation that will provide for the social and economic benefits to which these artists are entitled?

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Edwards (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this question was raised earlier today on a point of order having to do with questions about phase two of the copyright legislation. I can tell the hon. member that the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture of which she is a member will shortly be seized with the issue if it is not already. It has the authority under the House rules to identify its own areas of study and the minister is anxiously awaiting the labors of that committee.

Mr. Speaker, it is ironic that the Parliamentary Secretary would answer in that way. He knows that we did not one, but two studies on the status of the artist, the taxation of the artist, and he was chairman of the committee at that time.

Mr. Speaker, my second question is as follows: It has always been recognized that one has the right to be paid once a job is finished. This is a fundamental human right. Nowadays, in the 20th century, in a so-called civilized country like Canada, hundreds of performers do not receive money that is rightfully theirs, in return for the reproduction and sale of their work, and the government is not doing anything about it.
Mr. Speaker, I want the Minister to tell us here and now, in the presence of all the great artists with us here today, exactly when he intends to table phase two of the copyright bill that would give them the legal means to collect the fruits of their work.

Mr. Speaker, first I would like to thank the hon. member for her question. Today is of course a very important day for members of the Canadian arts community who have come to meet Members of Parliament and the ministers. I met them this morning, and we discussed these issues, with particular emphasis on two aspects: the status of artists and copyright phase two. The hon. member knows perfectly well that the government is defining its approach, objectives and goals in close co-operation with

Oral Questions
the Canadian arts community. We have advisory committees that are travelling across Canada to identify the areas the government will deal with. I can give the House the assurance that the government's commitment as expressed and approved by the Prime Minister, is well-known to the arts community.

Mr. Speaker, bouquets and flowery words since 1984 have not changed one bit the status of the artist nor the legislation that we wanted in phase one of copyright.
It is now clear that artists, orchestras, dance troupes, opera companies, playwrights and regional theatres will face severe financial hardship because of the government's proposed goods and services tax.
That 9 per cent will strain to a breaking point the cultural activities which employ thousands of people in Canada. Does the minister not realize that the GST could be the straw that breaks the artists backs? Why is the minister sitting on the sidelines while his colleague, the Minister of Finance, is busy sinking the cultural ships of this country?

Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member wants to show her teeth, I will have to answer that since 1984, there has never been a government in this country that did so much for structural reform in the cultural domain.
Hear, hear.

Since 1984, we have created task forces on the arts and on copyright. We identified policy, and as far as legislation is concerned, we started to do what not a single government had done previously, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, my question is also for the Minister of Communications. Over 70 per cent of English language television programming in Canada originates in the United States. This country allows Americans to sell their product to Canadian networks at a fraction of production costs. That is dumping and that is unfair to Canadian artists.
Foreigners are not allowed to do that, say, with their wheat. They are not allowed to do it with clothing. They are not allowed to do it with boots. Why is television programming treated any differently from other products that enter the Canadian market-place from abroad? My question for the minister is this: why are Americans allowed to dump their television programming on the Canadian market-place thereby undermining Canadian cultural sovereignty and taking much needed jobs away from Canadian artists?
Mr. Speaker, the answer is very simple. It is because what we have now is the law that you passed in 1968. That is the one we want to change.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the minister responsible for culture and communications. Many Canadians do not realize that most artists in this country do not get their full pay cheque after the first production of their work. Many Canadians do not realize this, Minister. And the question that I have to ask you is: do you realize how insulting it is for people to watch their work on television when they are not being paid? How would you like it not to get your full pay cheque?
Order!

Mr. Speaker, we are now making structural changes to correct a vast number of problems we have identified in the cultural sector. When Lemeac, a publishing company, went bankrupt, which government helped the creative arts? The Government of Canada, Mr. Speaker.
Tomorrow in Toronto, I will have the pleasure to announce increased revenues for Canadian writers under the public library utilization program, and that was arranged by this government, with the agreement of my colleagues and especially of the Prime Minister. And we intend to continue in that vein, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Right Hon. Prime Minister, and I must say that I am sad to have to ask the Prime Minister this question. He will be aware from the press

reports this morning that Senator Cogger was found to be in breach of the Parliament of Canada Act. As a result of access to information, it was found that Senator Cogger was in clear contravention of the laws of Parliament by sending a bill to the Federal Business Development Bank for legal services.
The Prime Minister will be aware, very aware, that under section 14 of the Parliament of Canada Act, it is illegal for a senator to do business with a Crown corporation. Now that he has been informed of this act by Senator Cogger, has he done the right thing, the decent thing, and approached his friend and asked for his resignation?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the member is referring to reports alleging impropriety on the part of an hon. senator. That should be dealt with in the other place.
I understand that the hon. senator is making a statement, at this very moment, in the other place. I think that is the appropriate forum for that issue to be dealt with.

Mr. Speaker, since the Prime Minister essentially appoints the senators, I think it is only appropriate that he respond.
It was only after access to information that we were able to determine that Senator Cogger, in fact, had collected money from this Crown corporation. I hope we do not have to go and do an examination of every single Crown corporation to determine where else Senator Cogger was collecting funds.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I want to proceed with very great care. What we have in front of us-and I ask hon. members to pay attention-is apparently something which has appeared in the newspaper. The hon. minister has said that the gentleman involved, who is a member of the other place, is making a statement this afternoon.
I am very reluctant to let questions go too far for fear they become, by way of their preamble, accusations to which there may or may not be any evidence whatever, and certainly, under the principles of fair play, if the hon. member of the Senate is going to make a statement this afternoon, that statement ought to be heard.
Oral Questions
I would ask the hon. House Leader for the New Democratic Party, who is very experienced in this place, to proceed with very great care.

Mr. Speaker, I will proceed with very great care. I appreciate the comments that you have made.
The question is that this issue only arose after this information was provided through using access to information on this one Crown corporation. We do not want to go through every Crown corporation using the same process to find to what extent the senator has been involved.
I am asking the Prime Minister-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I very much regret feeling that I am going to have to go on to the next questioner, because the preamble is becoming an allegation, at least it is an implied allegation and I think that the obligation of the Speaker in this place is to be extraordinarily careful.
I have said in the past that there has to be, and there is, a duty upon members to ask questions. But especially in this day of television a preamble can be very close to a charge, and there is another place to make a charge. There is, of course, instant publication of this. I think that somehow the Speaker has to find a way that respects fair play and, at the same time, allows questions to be asked.
There is another hon. minister here who is ultimately responsible for that particular Crown corporation. If the member wants to put a question to the minister with respect to the Crown corporation then I invite him to do so.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the sensitivity of this issue and I want to be very careful. I simply want to say that we will await the senator's comments in the other place and would expect, of course, that if the accusations are correct, that not only does he have a $200 fine per day to pay, which would be about $140,000 now, but we would expect the full amount to be paid back.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
What I am asking hon. members to respect is that if hon. members have charges to make there is an appropriate place to make them in this House. There are consequences that go with it. There may be more questions on this and I would ask hon. members to proceed with fairness and care.
The hon. member for York Centre.

Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the minister who you identified as being responsible, indeed, for the Federal Business Development Bank. I want, before asking, to underline that whatever happens in the other place, there is no doubt that ministers here have responsibility for the operations of the corporations under their jurisdiction.

My question for the Minister is as follows: Did he get in touch today with officials at the Federal Business Development Bank to find out whether this payment had been made, as indicated in information released by the government, which shows for instance that $72,000 was sent to this law office, attention of the senator? I would like to know whether the minister is prepared to ask the bank to recover these funds.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, yes, I have been in contact with the Federal Business Development Bank and was informed that the Federal Business Development Bank has hired the law firm of Lapointe Rosenstein on many occasions going back over a couple of decades.

Mr. Speaker, the documents which that department released show that payments made to that firm of lawyers were made to the attention of Senator Cogger and there is no doubt about that, it is in the minister's own documents. Therefore, I am not satisfied that the answer the minister has given about what years and years of work may have been done by a firm. Is the minister looking this into and does he agree that these payments should be reclaimed by the Federal Business Development Bank?

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Federal Business Development Bank representatives informed me that they made the decision to hire Lapointe Rosenstein on this occasion as they have on other occasions. They hire companies across the country. They received the work for which they contracted and they satisfied the invoices. competition. rules. He said that the changes must reflect "federal budget restraints".

Mr. Speaker, in conclusion I want to ask the House to think very seriously about the idea of a special task force or a parliamentary committee to look at changing our taxation system so that a very important part of that system is what we call the greening of Canada or the greening of the planet. We need a system of sticks and carrots that will motivate not only corporations, but also individuals, to consume and produce products that are going to be of benefit to the environment of Canada. I think we should be doing that.
There is so much we can do with the tax system in this country in terms of the kind of country we want. If we are to have incentives to keep this country cleaner and penalties to make sure that industry does not pollute our rivers, our lakes and our air, I think we would all be better off for it.
It is a new idea being pushed by the member for Skeena that we should have a very important principle in our taxation system namely, that we have the eco-tax or the green tax. I think it is something that we should study. I am sure that we can get all three parties looking very seriously at the problem, and perhaps we can make
Supply
a very important change that would be as important in principle as the principle of ability to pay or of making sure that our taxation is not regressive but progressive.
Let us take a look at that in our taxation system.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this debate today. I want to focus my comments for the next 10 minutes on the impact of an ecologically sound green tax system on transportation because, in this vast country of ours, no policy that we develop should be in isolation of transportation.
We and my colleague from Regina-Lumsden in particular, who has fought this battle for many, many years, have talked about and believe in the concept of a transportation system that is interconnected, a multimodal system wherein you maximize each of the modes of travel to the extent possible within the geographic realities, but more importantly in the context of this debate, in terms of environmental realities and in terms of the use of fossil fuels and other forms of fuel.
Just a few moments ago in this House I raised a question about the environmental impact of the cuts to VIA Rail. We were told this morning by the officials of the department, the person who is in charge of surface transportation, that the seven-page initial environmental assessment that was conducted by the Department of Transport, by her and a gentleman who comes from the economics branch of transport-we have a transportation specialist and an economic specialist deciding on environmental matters. It is like the Minister of Finance making decisions about VIA Rail and transportation matters. But we will come back to that at another point.
First of all, they did say that x number of people will be shifted from the rail passenger mode, which is one of the most environmentally friendly modes of travel, particularly in terms of the large scale movement of people within a country, to see what the impact would be. They know how many people will take their car rather than the train, and how many people will get on a bus or how many people will get on a plane. But what they did not do is to then quantify that. If we have one million more car trips per year, which is what they are suggesting it will be the result of their decision on VIA Rail, although even that is in dispute, that means one million more cars

Supply
driving probably an average of 250 kilometres which I think is the suggested norm.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
speechtext: No, it doesn't.

I am not talking about one million new cars, I am not talking about trips that would not have otherwise occurred. But what they did not do was the next logical step. In any environmental assessment the most logical step is to measure the impact on the environment. How many more kilograms or kilotonnes of nitrous oxide or carbon dioxide would be emitted in the atmosphere? They did not do that, Mr. Speaker. They just said that one million more car trips, really will not have much of an impact so let's not bother doing a full environmental assessment. Part of the reason why we of the New Democratic Party put forward this motion today is to make the point that we have to treat our world a lot better than we are now.
Any kind of government policy, in this case on taxation, but also on transportation, should have as its uppermost concern the impact on the environment. Let us hope it is in terms of how we can lessen the impact on the environment, not how we can add more like this decision on VIA Rail has done. In this great country of ours, which is such a vast magnificent land, many people live in a very narrow corridor next to the Canada-U.S. border, with some fingers of development in the northern territories. In northwestern Ontario we have had to build around Lake Superior and the Great Lakes in order to get from east to west. We need an integrated system.
It does not make sense for people to be flying from Toronto to Ottawa or Toronto to Montreal, or Montreal to Ottawa when for substantially less money, fuel and land, and much less pollution, we could be using high speed electrified rapid transit between those main communities. Given the congestion of Pearson International Airport, which is not going to be solved by a new terminal, it will be quicker, downtown to downtown, to travel by rail between these cities. Think of the atmosphere, Mr. Speaker. I know that you travel on the trains from time to time. Consider how much easier it is to do business in that particular corridor with the high-tech we now have. On the train we can use cellular phones and have a desk away from home, so to speak. You arrive in a much less frazzled state. We can do with that kind of thing.
It makes sense in some of the regions of the country to use rail, to link Thunder Bay and Dryden for example, or Cape Breton and Halifax, rather than air for these short distances. There are many options for environmentally friendly forms of transport.
That is on the passenger side. What about the freight side? As a country we have to be able to move both raw materials and finished goods. Right now we do it on the basis that because of the high cost of transportation, those people who are farther away will pay more.
From an economic standpoint, dare I say it, we could change a couple of policies and follow the lead of the private sector. Some of the major department stores have what they call a regional pricing policy. We all get the fliers from Sears or Eatons and see that a fridge in Thunder Bay is priced the same as the one in Toronto. We have done it with beer in Ontario. We do it with milk in other provinces. We are required, by the company policy, to include transportation costs in the over-all price so it becomes part of their cost of doing business. Therefore, it is averaged out so that that fridge can be sold in every community at the same price.
One might ask what that has to do with an environmental tax. It has everything to do with it. We are crowding so many people into the golden horseshoe of southern Ontario, mainly because that is where the markets are, the people buy the finished goods. Therefore it makes sense, given the Canadian economy as it is structured now, to locate the plants there. So that means more people come to the golden horseshoe to work and therefore create more demand, and on and on and on. A transportation policy should reflect the environment and land use planning. We so often forget that land use planning is an important environmental consideration.
I listened with interest to an open line CBC program last week on which a well known author, who is also a farmer, was talking about the impact of the paving over of the agricultural land in southern Ontario. That by itself reduces the emissions of oxygen into the atmosphere, the ability of this planet to recycle its air, to clean it and to put it back out in a form that is suitable for human beings.
We could mix all these together and have an environmental tax system under which there is no tax or lesser tax on environmentally friendly things. For example, what if we exempted bicycles from sales taxes, from manufacturers taxes, to lower their price so that more
October 31, 1989

and more people could afford to use that extremely non-polluting form of transportation? We could electrify. The reality in this country is that by themselves CN or CP or VIA Rail, whatever is left of it by the time this government is finished, on their own cannot justify electrification because of the high up-front costs, but if the government was to do it we would not only save in the environment, we would save in terms of fossil fuels and we would promote a healthier planet.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with each passing day Canadians are more aware of and concerned with the state of the environment. More and more they realize that life on earth is predicated upon a delicate and complex fabric of ecologic systems. As humans we are at the same time a product of that environment, a major cause of its present state and a determining element of its future evolution. Each calory of energy used, each ton of mineral mined and processed by our technologies, each crop planted and harvested impacts in some way on the environment. From time immemorial the earth has provided the basic ingredients that are essential to life, namely air, water, food and heat. Those resources also are a global environment capital drawn upon by every economic activity, every development project. And, perhaps more importantly still, the earth sets the natural limits of economic development and life itself.
Mr. Speaker, it would be a total delusion to believe that we can escape environmental features and processes that are quite independent from human actions. The bottom line is that nature deals the cards and establishes the rules of the game.

In the last few generations the capacity of man to alter the global ecosystem has increased dramatically with increases in population and rapid advances in technology. World economic activity, for example, has increased 20-fold since 1900. As a result, many of man's activities are taxing the capacities of our global ecosystem beyond its limits. Each year we dump five billion tonnes of C02 in the atmosphere, consume 40 per cent of the planet's
Supply
biomass and the amount of fossil fuel it took the planet about one million years to create.
While global economic activity has expanded rapidly and living standards have improved enormously in the developed world, global poverty and population growth remain a fundamental problem. Global population is projected to double by 2050. Eight-five per cent of this will join the majority of the world's population which lives in poverty today and aspires to a better quality of life. Whether the global economy and the global environment can accommodate these hopes is perhaps the greatest challenge of our time.
Without a systematic framework for addressing these stresses, it is unlikely to be any relief for our global ecosystem. As the 21st century approaches, the outlook is for more and more demands on our planet's environmental resources as the global economic system seeks to meet the needs and aspirations of the growing world population. This will put at risk not only the capacity of our planet to sustain economic growth, but its capacity to sustain life. Future generations will pay dearly if we do not act now.

Mr. Speaker, when thus describing our environmental problems, one might think they are far remote from concerns of the Canadian people and that individual efforts are futile. However, neither perception is true. The problems that directly concern Canadians, for instance air pollution in our cities, Great Lakes water quality, climatic changes, ozone layer depletion, all those problems are symptomatic of larger problems deriving from the complex process of environmental interactions at the continental or global level.
It is equally erroneous to believe we are powerless as individuals. The way we use the natural environment is the result of countless day-to-day decisions made by individuals, corporations and governments. Whether this involves setting the thermostat and deciding how to use water or dispose of household garbage, managing effluents or building new industrial facilities or determining government economic policy, all those decisions have a cumulative impact on the environment. If the global environment today is threatened, it is because in making

Supply
those decisions we failed to consider the costs of pollution to the environment and our environmental heritage. Indeed, we treated the environment as a gift of nature.

We have not been blind to the need for action. There have been some important successes in dealing with pollution problems. Through the combined actions of individuals, corporations, interest groups and governments, sulphur dioxide emissions in Canada have fallen by almost 50 per cent since 1974, while lead levels have fallen by over 50 per cent. In many cases, however, these responses tended to be reactions to a crisis or problem situation, sometimes focusing entirely on clean-up. More than ever we realize the need to anticipate a problem and prevent its occurrence.
What is needed to cope with our emergency environmental challenges is not more rhetoric, not meaningless resolutions. What is needed is a fundamental change in the way we make decisions at all levels of society. We must begin to integrate environmental considerations into the day-to-day decisions we make as individuals, as corporations, and as governments. We must begin to treat the environment like the scarce and unique resource that it is; an ecosystem that is essential to the sustainability of development and life itself. This is what sustainable development is all about, changing behaviour, changing the way we see the environment, and its relationship to our activities. And that is how we will move from a reliance on reactive solutions to preventive solutions.
Each of us has a responsibility and a role as a decision-maker in changing behaviour and the behaviour of those around us. Globally, Canada has a responsibility as a steward of a significant fraction of the world's environmental resources and as a source of global ecosystem stress. This means we must look to a response that is both domestic and international in scope and demonstrates much needed leadership. Individuals, businesses, and governments have an important stewardship role as property owners and users of environmental resources.

However, governments bear an additional responsibility. A good part of the natural resources used by our economy are outside the market system and therefore considered a free product or service.
Normal market forces do not provide sufficient incentive to make environmentally sound decisions. Since the market is not able to provide a decision-making framework for responsible measures-

Mr. Speaker, Canadians expect the federal government to play a leading role on the environment. The government is meeting this challenge eagerly, and, in the spirit I announced several weeks ago, the government is now preparing an environmental action plan for Canada consisting of a national framework for implementing sustainable development.
Mr. Speaker, we know that the environment is a "hot" issue, a subject of concern in Canada and throughout the world. We know that governments are forced to react to the situation.
That is why the government decided several months ago now to task my department and all those departments represented on the environment committee with preparing a comprehensive environmental action plan for the next five years. We all know that we need comprehensive policies, additional measures and more resources.
Mr. Speaker, I shall vote against the motion before us, not because I believe that the government does not need
October 31, 1989

more resources: I do believe we need more. But, Mr. Speaker, I believe that the concept of an extra tax for the environment must be part of an approach that includes new environmental policies with new fiscal policies and harmonizes them, and that it must be perceived as such. All this will be in the action plan that will be presented to the government and made public in the spring.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with care to the remarks of the minister. It seems to me that he is hedging. He is not saying that he is opposed or that the government is opposed to a green tax system. It is a bit of a wait and see attitude.
As the minister knows, many countries around the world and very much across Europe have already introduced carbon taxes. They have already been introduced in Japan. Many of these green system taxes have been demonstrated to be highly beneficial. Not only do you reduce your energy consumption, but at the same time you are reducing the amount of pollution and in fact you are creating commodities. You are creating jobs at a much faster rate than under our existing archaic tax system.
I would just like to get clarification from the minister. Does he think that the approach being taken by his colleague, the Minister of Finance, in applying the new proposed 9 per cent GST to recycled paper at the same rate as to virgin paper is environmentally appropriate? I think the minister knows that a green tax system can be put to a wide range of uses, whether it is on recycled paper, on bicycles versus automobiles, or on canoes versus motor boats, or whatever. It will make for a cleaner environment, lower costs, lower energy use, less pollution, and full employment.
What kind of a recipe would any government be looking for that would bring in a more regressive form of taxation, self-admitted by the Minister of Finance, when other countries around the world have picked up and cobbled together different pieces of a green tax system? Does the minister not really want to stand up today and say he supports a green tax system, that now is the time to bring it in, and that we cannot wait any longer?

Mr. Speaker, taxes will always be needed for one main purpose-to raise money. The government needs money. The reason for
Supply
which governments have been created is to pool the resources of a nation in order to address the national and global problems of a nation.
This being said, we in this government think that we now have a new challenge in front of us, an international challenge, a national challenge. This challenge will call for new and additional resources. The problem is of such a magnitude that it will require the government to devise new fiscal policies. The GST question has no direct link with what we are doing in environment. GST is there to rationalize the way taxes are raised in Canada. This must be done. This has been the objective of our government. No government before has had the courage to do it. We had this courage because we think it is necessary. We did not do it to be popular. We did it because we think it is our duty.
Apart from that, we think we need more money for the environment. The way to raise that money is not necessarily something to do with one more tax. It is something to do with the framework of a new approach wherein, as the member has very eloquently said, we have to mesh the environmental purpose and the money raising purpose. This can be done. I am sure it will be done.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the minister a question. Given his concerns rightfully expressed about global warming, why has his government cut energy efficiency research and development grants and programs by 91 per cent?

It is a matter of philosophy, a matter of perception of what the problem is. This government does not believe that all the money spent on the environment must come from the public purse.
Recently, I had the opportunity to announce the creation of a fund to clean up orphan sites. One of the main conditions is that provinces must, in return, implement a legislative and regulatory mechanism in order to make it compulsory for companies to clean up 950 other sites. I give that example to show that the money will not come exclusively from new taxes and energy consumption measures, but also from the application of the polluter pays principle.
So it is obvious that, in our action plan, there will be a very strong emphasis on energy conservation measures, but energy conservation does not create energy. Obviously, that is where we must start, and that is exactly

what we will do. As we look at possible ways to conserve energy, we must also find ways to create energy.

Mr. Lee Clark (Brandon-Souris) Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to participate in today's debate, particularly with respect to the fact that daily we are becoming increasingly aware of the deteriorating nature of the environment. There are front page stories and television news items. Literally Canadians and other people around the world are being bombarded with a litany of old problems getting worse and new problems becoming more evident.
There have been tremendous implications for us as a government and as a country in terms of our domestic policy and with respect to our international relations with other nations and other governments. Later on this afternoon my colleague, the hon. member for Fredericton-York-Sunbury, will be speaking with respect to some of the matters to which the Government of Canada has responded vis-a-vis domestic policy.
I would like to look for a while this afternoon at some of the very, very important developments which have occurred in international arenas. To a very real extent the crisis of the environment is a global crisis, and the solutions must be found both outside our boundaries as well as inside.
As you know very well, Mr. Speaker, the United Nations-sponsored Brundtland commission issued a new agenda just a short time ago saying that the planet needs "a new era of environmentally sound economic development". That report said from now on-and I think most governments including ours have echoed that conclusion-we must have policies and economic positions based upon the concept of sustainable development. We must ensure that in future environmental decisions are a first thought in the decision-making process rather than an afterthought as they were all too often in the past.
We must change, as the Minister of the Environment said just the other day. We will have to tailor and change our lifestyles to fit the ecological realities of this new world in which we live. It may affect the way in which we grow food, harvest trees and generate power. We will obviously have to reduce the pollution that changes the
atmosphere and endangers our food and water supplies. We will have to protect our all too critical resources such as the farm land, the forests and the wildlife from overuse.
I come from Brandon-Souris in the province of Manitoba. We are all too aware of the fact that we have had drought for two years in succession. There is a growing amount of concern that it might be one of the first results of global warming.
We must favour types of economic development which fall within this planet's ability to absorb our wastes and to renew its resources. To do that we will have to link economic decisions and environmental impacts, whether we are making household purchases, industrial development decisions or forming government policy at the federal, provincial or the municipal level.
The question before us, however, is not whether the Government of Canada is prepared to respond to the key environmental problems that we face either as Canadians or as citizens of the world, which clearly we are. The question before us is whether or not we are simply prepared to put our eggs in one basket, in this case the basket of the so-called green tax, or whether we believe that we must develop a comprehensive national strategy in order to address all aspects of environmental issues.
We believe that there must be that comprehensive action plan to which the minister has alluded. We have given notice of our intention to act. We have indicated our willingness to translate the concept of sustainable development into concrete reality.
I think Canadians understand that some of the most compelling of the problems facing us are global, transboundary. We as a government understand therefore that we are going to resolve the problems, whether they be with respect to the depletion of the ozone layer, global warming or acid rain; that we are going to have to secure the co-operation of governments outside our own country.
I am proud of the activity that has occurred in recent years in which Canada has played an integral part. For example, we were the first nation to ratify the Vienna Convention for the protection of the ozone layer. This government took a lead role in developing and adopting
October 31, 1989

the Montreal Protocol on substances that deplete the ozone layer.
I was proud, if I may say so, as an individual member of Parliament to head our delegation to the Helsinki Convention last May where the nations of the world took further steps, recognizing that the Montreal Protocol in itself would be inadequate to rectify the crisis facing the ozone layer.
We agreed in Montreal to a partial reduction of chlorofluorocarbons by the year 2000. We as a government and other governments throughout the world now understand that there must be a total ban on the use of CFCs by 1999 or earlier.
In 1988 Canada hosted the Toronto Conference on the Changing Atmosphere, an important international conference with real implications for global security. In February of this year we followed that with a meeting of legal and policy experts where we developed proposals for a convention for the protection of the atmosphere. These initiatives have placed Canada in the foreground of international environmental diplomacy.
The Canada-United States Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement was renewed in November of 1987, providing stronger control over toxic substances entering the Great Lakes. Fulfilling a promise made in the Speech from the Throne the minister announced just recently $125 million as part of the five-year Great Lakes action plan.
Although we understand that the action plan is going to require the co-operation of provincial and municipal governments and industry if that cesspool, if one can use that term, of the Great Lakes is to be clean, what was announced just recently by the federal government was an important first step. It will have to be one of many.
Canada signed the Basel Convention which puts in place an international regime to govern the transboundary movement of hazardous wastes. This will prevent in the future the embarrassing situation of hazardous wastes being dumped as we have seen in the past in developing countries.
More recently, the Commonwealth heads of government issued a strong endorsement of sustainable devel-
Supply
opment. These accomplishments demonstrate our commitment to the environment. I believe we have been among world leaders in reducing threats to global environment.
Over the past 10 years, however, probably no single issue has been more important to Canadians with respect to international consequences than acid rain. The progress this government has made in that regard demonstrates our commitment to reducing the problem of acid rain and our commitment to ensuring better air quality for Canadians today, tomorrow and in the future.
Mr. Speaker, if you remember in 1984 there were no specific emission controls in place. Funding for vital acid rain research was about to lapse. Emission standards for new cars and trucks had not been changed for almost 10 years. Significant amounts of lead were still being used in gasoline in Canada.
Since 1984 we have reached an agreement with the seven most easterly provinces with respect to reduction of sulphur dioxide emissions. Those emissions have been reduced by some 40 per cent now, and it is clear that we will reach our objective of 50 per cent by 1994.
Loans have been made available to large emissions sources, to companies such as Noranda which have met their objectives for the reduction of sulphur dioxide emission reductions. Funds have been made available to assist in the development of new technologies.
Reduced allowable emissions from automobiles have been changed on two different occasions-in 1987 and in a very important agreement in Charlottetown last week where it was agreed we would adopt California standards by 1994. A decision was also made to eliminate the use of lead in gasoline by 1990 and to increase the excise tax on leaded gasoline in the meantime.
All these instances, plus a continuing effort on the part of Canada to work closer together with the United States to ensure that acid rain will be reduced, are evidence of first the recognition on the part of this government that the threat to our environment is global in nature and will require the co-operation of international governments, and that the federal government must work closely together with the provinces. We must come up with a long needed and much overdue comprehensive action plan of which perhaps the proposal that is

October 31, 1989
Supply
before us today may indeed be a part. I would not be able to anticipate that.
Certainly what I think is evident is that to preserve the environment from some of the dangers that we have so readily inflicted in the past and to ensure that the damages are reduced in the future requires a comprehensive and co-operative approach in which I hope all members of this House as well as all governments in Canada will participate. I hope the end result we see will be a better environment for our children, our grandchildren, and their children and grandchildren.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the hon. member whether he believes that pollution control devices should be subject to the goods and services tax.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think, as all members of this House know, the proposed goods and services tax is a long overdue response on the part of this government to the inadequacies of a manufacturers' sales tax which has been in place in Canada since 1924.
If I understand correctly when members on that side of the House in the Official Opposition had responsibility for government, which they did for many years, they looked on occasion at the possible abolition of the manufacturers' sales tax but, for whatever reason they chose, they decided not to proceed.
What the government is proposing today with the goods and services tax is something which is obviously not politically advantageous to us. I may say that sometimes I often hear from constituents who say to me as a politician, to the government of which I am a part: "Why do you not take tough decisions? Why do you not provide the kind of leadership which Canadians are seeking?"
I would suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the hon. member that the proposed goods and services tax is clearly an example of a government deciding that it must act in the interests of the nation as a whole.
All the polls tell us that what we propose is clearly not done in order to incur political favour. You need not be a political scientist to know, when you look at the statistics, that Canadians like other people throughout the world do not enjoy either new taxes. Nor do they enjoy direct taxes that are highly visible. I see in the goods and services tax an attempt to rectify an old problem, one
that has been here in Canada, one that has not worked well since 1924.
Speaking in general terms some 75,000 businesses have been affected by that tax. There are some 22,000 different tax arrangements. There is an estimated $2 billion in tax revenue that legally belongs to the Government of Canada that is not being collected.
I would suggest that we take that $2 billion, assuming we could collect it now under the goods and services tax which would be far more difficult for people to escape than otherwise before-and I would mention to members opposite that they have often criticized the government for permitting loopholes through which people can escape their obligation to pay tax-give it to the Minister of the Environment and permit him to do what he would wish to do. Not only would we have a very effective comprehensive action plan in place within the next 12 to 24 months. He would also have the kind of resources necessary to do the job in such a way that all members of this House would applaud.
Mr. Speaker, did the parliamentary secretary to the minister just announce that there is $2 billion being given out of the goods and services tax to the Minister of the Environment?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
What I announced, however, and I think the member probably knows this, is that the manufacturers' sales tax has worked so inefficiently that there has been on a year by year basis in essence $2 billion that was traditionally due to the Government of Canada which has not been collected because of the inefficiencies in that particular tax.
What I said to the hon. member was that that revenue by law properly belongs to the Government of Canada. I suggested that if we had those kinds of additional revenues in place we would have far more resources. I think all members here would agree that the environment should be higher on our priority list. We would have the resources available to do some of the things we believe are necessary.
At this point in time the Government of Canada must spend $28 billion, $29 billion, $30 billion a year on interest alone on a debt which has accumulated since the early 1970s. It takes almost 33 per cent of our government revenues alone to go to interest on money spent in
October 31, 1989

the past. We have limited our capacity to respond to the degradation which has already existed.
We live in the midst of a crisis, a crisis that is twofold. First of all, we have inherited as a people a degraded environment as a result of the failures of Canadians for decades. Governments as well as individuals have contributed to that degradation through some sort of failure on their part.
In addition, the second part of the crisis which is so significant is that the growth of the national debt at a time when there was no economic rationale for its development, particularly during buoyant years of the 1970s, has contributed to an economic malaise and almost an economic bankruptcy within this country to the extent that they cannot respond to the environmental crisis which is ours.
We are now at a stage where we are well aware of the problem, where we have the political will to address it, where I think to a large degree we have the co-operative support of not only members of this House but governments throughout the land, federal, provincial and municipal, that are strapped with the fact that they lack the economic resources that they would wish.
If the goods and services tax can succeed in reforming the tax base to the extent that it becomes a fairer and more equitable tax with fewer loopholes and the moneys which are legitimately the Government's of Canada are collected more effectively and distributed more equitably than they were in the past, then I would suggest that that indeed would be good for the country even though it may not contribute to our political well-being in the short term.

Mr. Speaker, we have just heard from the Minister of the Environment a difficult and repetitive bilan of the state of the Canadian and the world environment.
I feel somewhat frustrated because it seems to me that time and time again we hear from this minister how bad the situation is, and we have heard his rather flowery rhetoric on this subject on dozens of occasions, but in actual fact his capacity to encourage change is completely lacking. I am frustrated, as millions of Canadians must
Supply
be frustrated, when I hear the Minister of the Environment and the Prime Minister claim that their first priority is cleaning up the environment, when he actually has the audacity to stand in his place today and vote against the principle of a green tax.
The principle that has been put forward in the votable motion by the hon. member for Skeena is in fact a wide-ranging motion which would incorporate the notion of green taxes into the Canadian economy. I fail to understand the logic of the Minister of the Environment who claims to be an environmental advocate when every single one of his actions since taking office has gone in the opposite direction.
He avoided the question about how this government has cut back drastically on alternative energies and on conservation research. He claimed that he wanted a public-private sector mix. How does he rationalize that statement with his own budget document which shows that his government is going to be spending $5 billion to develop energy megaprojects which they know contribute to the burning of fossil fuel that is creating a situation in which our climate is warming at the same time as the total package for alternative energies is pathetically small and cut on a daily basis?
Friends of the Earth analysed the financial objectives of the government in relation to energy policy. They showed, quite rightly, that for every dollar spent on energy conservation the government is setting aside $19 to spend on development of fossil fuels which lead to global warming. In fact the actual amount cut in alternative energies and energy consumption in conservation since 1984 will reach 93 per cent within the next few years. The actual amount of money the government has set aside for conservation unrenewables, according to a document published recently by Friends of the Earth, is actually $250 million and falling-I believe it has actually been reduced a further $60 million since that time-as compared with $5 billion set aside for fossil fuel megaprojects.
I do not know whether the Minister of the Environment thinks Canadians are stupid. I do not know whether he takes us all for fools. But how can he continue to insist that his government has a plan for global warming, that his government has a plan for reducing the amount of fossil fuel that we bum, when his own department along with the Department of Energy are unwilling to

October 31, 1989
Supply
even assume target dates for fossil fuel reduction for this country?
It came as no surprise that California emission standards were announced by the Ontario Minister of the Environment at the national conference in Prince Edward Island a few days ago. It seems that when you talk about leadership in the environment in this country the Ontario Minister of the Environment is taking the leadership. We have the federal minister who followed up with a recommendation originally.

A recommandation from the premier of Quebec encouraging the adoption of the California emission standards.

But they did it after the United States had already decided to move in that direction.
I would like to ask the minister-and I would like him to speak to the people of Canada-about why a green tax is such a bad thing. He says he may not want to use tax policy to shape our conservation and consumption practices in this country. But he should admit right now that his own department in an internal document is examining the possibility of setting up emissions trading in the same way that is currently being endorsed by the Clean Air Act in the United States. He is examining a proposal which would turn pollution into a marketable commodity. That is how his government sees the market-place. They are going to be able to buy and sell pollution permits.
Instead of saying to companies that they should reduce their over-all level of pollution because it is going to be good for the air we breathe, it is going to be good for our children, it is going to be good for our country, he is actually examining the creation of a pollution permit which would permit Canadian companies to trade pollution rights among themselves. God forbid that we arrive at the day in this country when the right to pollute is a marketable commodity. That is exactly what is envisioned in the notion of having these pollution permits.
I know that the government likes to take ideas from its American counterparts. I know that that is currently one of the domestic provisions of the U.S. Clean Air Act. But I believe that in the past under successive Liberal governments Canada has shown a leadership role in
reduction of SO2 emissions. I would hate to see us follow in the footsteps of the United States where it concerns turning sulphur dioxide and other emissions into a commodity.
Canadians deserve better. Canadians want better. We only had to attend the meeting of the International Joint Commission at which for the first time in the joint study released by the Conserver Society and the IRPP, which is as a matter of fact as we speak making a presentation before the environment committee on global warming, to see for the very first time a link between airborne toxins and human brain damage.
I know that that biannual meeting of the International Joint Commission did not interest the minister. He would prefer to be studying water filtration problems in Paris. I can understand why he would not want to have been there for the launching of the IRPP report. It is the first time that we have actually drawn a link between actual brain damage in humans and airborne toxins.
Last summer I had the opportunity to go to Broughton Island. I had a chance to meet there with the city council of Broughton Island. It is a small community in the eastern Arctic that volunteered for a study of the effects of trace contaminants of PCBs.
Do you know what that study showed, Mr. Speaker? In the most pristine, untouched part of the world currently accessible only by plane, set up on the DEW Line in about 1960 essentially to service the needs of the military, the women in that community have PCBs in their mother's milk.
This minister and this government will not move to reduce the allowable burning of trace PCBs from 50 parts per million to 20 parts per million because, the minister says, the scientific data is inconclusive. The scientific data may be inconclusive for trace contaminants, but the scientific data for those women who have PCBs in their mother's milk is not inconclusive.
We actually heard during the Liberal caucus in Iqaluit that some mothers were so distraught about the situation that instead of feeding their children with their own mother's milk, they fed them with Coffeemate and the children suffered from malnutrition. They could not afford to pay the exorbitant price of fresh milk that comes in by plane and costs about $6 a litre in the store
October 31, 1989

in Broughton Island, so they fed their children with Coffeemate.
When the minister talks about developing a world protocol and about the international conventions, they are all extremely important and should be supported, but in our own country we have to act and we have to act now. That means we have to be prepared in the case of green taxes to look at examples that have been working for example in the European Community, with which the minister is very familiar and from which he likes to draw a lot of ideas. Why do we not look at what has been done in the European community or in Japan to cut back on the consumption of carbon fuels at the same time as we increase the awareness that there is a cost benefit relationship between pollution, taxation, and the GNP.
In the current move in Alberta to set up, at the latest count, almost nine or ten pulp and paper mills using old technology which would not be acceptable in Japan, why is it that we have not included in the cost benefit analysis the cost to the rivers and to the health and to the future of the people of the Northwest Territories, and the people who are living along the Athabasca and Slave River basins?
Why is it we have not moved with the recommendation that there be in fact an element of the GNP assessment specifically devoted to environmental degradation. Surely as trees are cut down across this country so there is a cost, short term and long term, that is being borne by ourselves and by our children. That cost is not currently reflected in the tax system, and that cost is not currently reflected in accounting principles adopted by the government.
What the hon. member for Skeena is recommending is that we be prepared to move in new and different directions.

For quite some time we have heard the Minister of the Environment's empty rhetoric on his good intentions with regard to the environment. But where was he, Mr. Speaker, when the PCB crisis broke out in Quebec? He was hiding in his cottage afraid to come out and take a stand. He did not want to show federal leadership on a national issue, just as he is now ready to reject the proposed tax system which would reflect more closely for

the Canadian people the cost of pollution and the cost of preservation.
We know full well that the tax system, for example, has been used for years to speed up corporate development. For instance, a company can claim depreciation when purchasing new equipment. It is a strategy adopted by several governments precisely to speed up development in our country. We have now got to the point where, in our own future, in my daughter's lifetime, temperatures in the Great Lakes are expected to rise so much over the next 50 years that winter in southwestern Ontario will be two to four weeks shorter. As Canadians, we can say that a shorter winter is a good thing but we have to consider the effect it will have on farmers and agriculture since, according to the Great Lakes report, Canadian farmers will have 50 per cent less moisture to work with.
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the House held a debate on the crisis facing family farms in Canada. We know that the tax issue is not the only major problem with which the farming community must come to grips, for it has to deal as well with rising temperatures and the world-wide warming trend which has become so obvious.
In that context the minister has little choice other than at least endorsing the principle of green taxation, much in the same way as he must support a federal government policy aimed at reducing grants awarded for megaprojects. At the same time, additional funds must be set aside for conservation technology and research on renewable resources.
Mr. Speaker, ever since this government took office the Minister of the Environment and his officials reduced by 93 per cent the money available for conservation and alternate energy projects, not to mention the fact that at the same time they are going to allocate $5 billion for megaprojects without first considering the possibility of cutting down on Canada's over-all energy requirements, along the line of well-established European conservation principles, for example.
So all I can say to the minister is that talk comes cheap, but why is he not prepared at least to consider the advisability of implementing green taxation such as they already have in a number of sectors in Europe and Japan and which seems to have a double impact. The first has to do with tax revenues, and the minister maintains that it is the only purpose of a tax system. The second impact can be seen in consumer habits. If as citizens, as federal

government, as provincial government, or as corporations we really want to distance ourselves-

I listened with interest to what the member for Hamilton East had to say. I was especially interested in that last part of her discourse because I, too, have great concern over those who talk about the environment but do not practise it.
Any time we ask a hundred people what is the most glaring issue of the day, their answer is it is the environment. However, if we followed those hundred people around for a day, we would find that a great percentage of them are polluting our environment. It seems to be a mindset; it is somebody else's problem and not theirs. They use environment unfriendly products; they throw their cigarette butts on the street; they wash their driveways down into the storm sewers without cleaning them up; they sneak burn their leaves; they take all the wrappings that they should not take at the fast food stores. I might ask the member when was the last time she refused some of the wrappers offered at the fast food drive-in. We should say no, we do not want them. We just want the food. We do not want all that environmentally unfriendly material.
I wonder what we are doing with our young people. I met with a number of school children just a week or so ago and they were talking about the environment. The environment is of great concern to them, but they do not seem to realize that they should be concerned about the environment through all they do.
Do we really have to throw money at this sort of thing and tax people? Do we have to use taxes to make them
October 31, 1989

think about the environment, those individuals who pollute our environment every day? I have concern about whether we have to tax them, or whether we should be using other means.
Members of Parliament themselves should show examples. Perhaps we should use some of the ways we have of communicating with the public, i.e. Householders and so on, wherein we could talk about the environment and what people individually could do to be helpful in not polluting our environment and not necessarily always have to look at dollars. Yes, we need dollars, but are there not other ways.
We as members of Parliament, the member from Hamilton included, should do something by communicating with our constituents and do a better job of communicating the need to being environmentally conscious and practise some of the more simplistic measures rather than constantly bombarding them with the more complex side. Not that we should not be concerned about all that, but individuals on the street need to be coaxed and cultured into being more environmentally conscious in everything they do all day long every day.
Ms Copps: My point, and I do not know if the member agrees with it, is I believe that the people are doing and are prepared to do much more than the politicians. The member mentioned fast food packaging. Who establishes packaging laws in this country? It is the federal ministry of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. It could move in and require that all packaging be produced in a material that is recycled. The federal ministry of Consumer and Corporate Affairs could move in and do that. What I am suggesting is that the public is prepared to do it, but we the politicians are not prepared to come forward with some innovative new approaches.
The federal government is not broke when it comes to the $5 billion it is setting aside for energy megaprojects, so it is a question of making choices.
Who chose to spend $5 billion on energy megaprojects and about $250 million or less on the renewables? That is a political choice of his government. It was his government that moved in 1984 to do away with the Canadian Home Insulation Program, probably one of the single best ways of permitting Canadians to insulate their homes so they would use less energy.

What is the intelligence of cancelling the Canadian Home Insulation Program and at the same time spending $5 billion on energy megaproject claiming it is in the effort to assure security of supply? Surely security of supply has to deal with not only getting new energy sources available, but also reducing the energy that we are using on an ongoing basis.

People in Europe or other countries who have not had the tremendous access to "unlimited energy supplies" that we have had in this country are more energy conscious.
