speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak today on the motion which asks the House to enact important changes to the present tax system. I must at the beginning of my remarks place the issue in its proper context. As the member for Trois-Rivieres, I feel the government has shown up to now that we are more than favourably disposed towards the environment and since 1984 we have done tremendous work in that regard and about the environmental situation our country and the world is in. I think we owe it all to our Right Hon. Prime Minister as well as to the Minister of the Environment we have had for five years.
There is always great danger, Mr. Speaker, when politicians and particularly managers of a country such as Canada try to mix apples and oranges. That is what this motion does today. It says on the one hand: We want to protect the environment, and on the other hand: Let us tax, let us use the tax system for the environment. That reminds me, and you will remember it too, Mr. Speaker, the pre-1984 tax measure called scientific research tax credit that cost not millions but billions of dollars to Canadians and did not in the end bring any scientific research to the country. We must be very careful. If, regarding environmental matters, a budget is allocated

October 31, 1989
Supply
to the Minister of Environment, his competent officials administer that budget, invest the money and develop proper policies, fine!
Mr. Speaker, I agree with that approach. But don't ask the Department of Finance, don't ask the tax experts, who are certainly not environmentalists, to make decisions on a tax for the environment. That is the problem, Mr. Speaker. Since 1984, we have established or re-established a tax system that works. We closed loopholes and removed tax shelters that existed when we came to power in 1984. We introduced a minimum income tax. We reduced the number of tax brackets from ten to three, as you know. We removed personal exemptions, basic exemptions, exemptions for the sick, and so forth, and we replaced those with a tax credit, the same amount for everybody, irrespective of income. We made the system fair and effective.
And now in Phase II of the tax reform, we will finally get rid of a 13 per cent manufacturer's sale tax and replace it with a 9 per cent goods and services tax, which will benefit all Canadians. This will be the last step towards an effective and valid tax system in this country, one that will make us competitive internationally. It is all very well to have a fiscal policy in this country, but that policy must also help our businesses, either to compete with imports or to export their products and compete on the international market. In both cases, our fiscal policy and our economic policy must be compatible and help Canadian business. Our tax system will now be complete. However, if we want to add a tax to deal with environmental problems, I can see the Opposition saying tomorrow or the day after: We should have a tax to deal with some other problem in another department, for instance, a special tax on transportation. The next day, the Opposition will tell me they need a special tax for the deficit. And in three, or four or five years, if we listen to the Opposition, if we introduce every single tax they ask for to deal with all these problems, our tax system will be in the same mess, it will be the same major problem we had when we came to power in 1984. That is why, Mr. Speaker, I think we must keep taxation and the environment separate.
Mr. Speaker, when we talk about improving the quality of life of our constituents, we must always be sure it will be in their best interests. A typical example Canadians will remember, as I said earlier, was the scientific research tax credit-some cases are still before the courts-where there was a terrific waste of taxpayer's
money without any benefit to the community. This was an example of bad management, and it certainly didn't do scientific research any good.
The Minister of the Environment, the Hon. Member for Lac-Saint-Jean (Mr. Bouchard) has acted responsibly on environmental issues. He has made firm commitments. We must not forget, when we are talking about the environment, that this is not a regional or a provincial issue but a federal issue, and also an international issue. At that level, the Prime Minister of Canada and the Minister of Environment have also acted responsibly, and that is very important. We must keep working at the international level because even if your own backyard is clean, if the neighbours don't clean theirs, it is very likely the bugs will migrate from their yards to yours. So as far as the environment is concerned, we must keep up the pressure, both internationally and nationally.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, you will realize that in the circumstances, I cannot agree with the motion as drafted.
As I said earlier, there have been some very substantial changes in our tax system since 1984. We have expanded the tax base, both for individuals and companies, so that everyone will pay his fair share of taxes. The same applies to capital gains. The same applies to the lifetime exemption on capital gains.
I don't think we should dismantle what we managed to build during the past five years, a system that has resulted in substantial dividends both for Canadians individually and for the quality of life in this country.
With the GST, all families with an income of $30,000 or less will be in a better position as far as taxes are concerned, meaning that once the system is in place in 1991, they will have more disposable income than they have now. They will be entitled to an annual tax credit of $275 per adult and $100 per child, to which may be added another tax credit, depending on individual or family income. Furthermore, businesses will be entitled to a maximum of $600 for completing the paperwork required in connection with the goods and services tax. You know as well as I do, Mr. Speaker, that the paperwork will not be significant. It will be just one 8 1/2 by 11-inch sheet the company will have to complete once a month. Monthly sales minus monthly purchases, and the difference multiplied by 9 per cent, and that amount is sent to us here at the federal government. Nine million Canadians will receive a cheque in December 1990. Before the goods and services tax is even in place, nine million Canadians will have received a cheque. That is not what
October 31, 1989

I would call a regressive consumer tax system but rather a just and fair system.
Moreover, we will further reduce by 1 per cent the personal income tax of Canadians who are in the middle tax bracket.
Then, Mr. Speaker, we will have an excellent tax system. And I don't think we should collect a green tax because if we do start with the environment, we will have to follow through with transport, fisheries, and so on. Departments have competent people to manage their budget, and we should give them the money they need to improve the quality of life for Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I heard comments in this House that I often hear when we want to introduce social and economic changes and change for the better of our world. I spent a number of years before I entered this Chamber in municipal governments, including chairing the committee that was responsible for dealing with sewers, garbage and river pollution, among other things. I guess I have a very down-to-earth view of some of the solutions that we need to pursue. It is very clear to me that we need to pursue intergovernmental solutions, not all at one level and not in isolation.
We need to recognize that municipalities are way ahead of us. We need to recognize that the people of Canada are way ahead of us as governments, as politicians and as leaders.
I want to address a number of areas in which we are not meeting our responsibilities or obligations. Every time there is a measure that is retrograde and counterproductive it is blamed on taxes. We are told we have to

What are we cutting? In many cases we are cutting the solutions to our problems. Rather than solving problems, we are creating new ones. The solutions to the world's problems and, to a large extent, our economic problems are in that research. Energy research within the federal government departments has been cut. How many millions of dollars are we spending on those vehicles? How are we using that purchasing power to exercise leadership in demanding the kinds of vehicles for government use that will help deal with the problem of global warming? The government has failed to use its economic power to demand the kinds of products in a variety of fields.
Through that leadership, in fact, we could be providing the incentive to industry to develop products that not only do less damage to the environment but delete less of the world's resources.
If we look at all levels of government, the power of that purchasing ability is multiplied severalfold. Municipal governments across this country spend 25 per cent more than the federal government on the purchase of goods and services and slightly less than the provincial governments. We as governments can triple our influence simply by what products we choose to purchase and what criteria we put on the product we buy. I am not tremendously optimistic that there will be that kind of comprehensive approach because in the last year, and as a member of the environment committee, I have seen very little indication that there is any high level of understanding.
Let us not talk about educating the public. They are educated far beyond us in terms of what they are doing, what they are prepared to do and what they are prepared to spend. If anything, they need information from government on how to carry out the motivation that they already have.
As I say, I am not optimistic. I listened with a great deal of concern to the debate in this House when one of my colleagues proposed that the Ministry of Industry, Science and Technology should include in its mandate responsibility for sustainable development. The minister dismissed it as basically hearts, flowers and music, something nice to have, but can live without. What does that have to do with the economy? Anybody who understands the principle of sustainable development understands that if we do not change the way we run our economy and do not develop economically in a way of our resources, we will have no resources on which to prosper.
I see the same approach in transportation. I see the Minister of Transportation who stands up in this House day after day in Question Period and says: "I can't afford to be concerned about the environment." If that is the government's attitude about its own operations and its own activities, I cannot believe that this is a government that is going to say to industrial polluters, "It is going to cost you but you are going to have to clean up."
We see it in department after department. The Minister of the Environment says that he is not responsible for environmental matters, that it is the responsibility of every department. When a department is challenged on its responsibilities for environmental matters within its area of operation it states that it is the responsibility of the Minister of the Environment. The other side of the House is going to have to get its act together or the world is going to fall apart.
I want to talk about the issue of intergovernmental co-operation. We have an ideal opportunity in this capital city of Canada to demonstrate how intergovernmental co-operation can work to ensure that transportation policies, land use policies, parks policies, activities of government are carried out not only in a way which does not damage the environment but would improve the quality of our environment and diminish our use of resources.

We have in this region three levels of government. Two provincial governments control what happens on both sides of the river. There are numerous municipal governments and the federal government. The federal government controls one third of the land mass in the national capital region and 30 per cent of the employment. Such influence on how a community develops gives one the power to work with the other levels of government to make substantial changes and demonstrate through our own national capital region how other cities in Canada and, indeed, around the world can become energy-conscious communities. Yet, not a 10-minute walk from Parliament Hill, the National Capital Commission is planning the development of the last major open space in the heart of this region. It is not paying attention to principles of sustainable development. It is designing a standard community in standard ways.
One of my colleagues has a private members' motion, which I certainly hope comes to the floor of this House, proposing that the NCC take the leadership and initiative to become responsible to co-ordinate and co-operate with an effort to use the nation's capital as a demonstration project for environmentally sustainable urban living.
It is not always a question of spending money. Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to speak in this debate this afternoon as a member of the Standing Committee on the Environment and as a supporter of the goods and services tax measure-as well.
The hon. member for Skeena has very cleverly combined the considerations of the environment and the taxation issue in a very interesting motion, one which I cannot support, but one which I nonetheless appreciate for the essence of its provocation and for the attention and emphasis which it brings both to the environment and to the tax issue.
Let me say that I support the environmental concerns of the hon. member for Skeena. I acknowledge and pay respect to his considerable knowledge about things environmental, and I share his concerns and his environmental goals but I must say that I differ considerably on how to accomplish and pay for the achievement of those goals.
On October 23, the hon. Minister of the Environment addressed the United Nations and said that we can speak to the environmental problem in rather simple ways. We can either move to develop sustainable economic and social practices or we can leave the problems to our children and hope that they are capable of solutions that escape us.
If the choice can be stated that simply, it does not mean a quick-fix single panacea like a green tax system, or some other socialist-oriented, profit-motive that I would fail to understand, but a comprehensive framework for action, a comprehensive strategy, and a financial strategy designed to provide the wherewithal by which government can carry out not just its environmental program but its entire program from which we may ultimately be able to initiate some environmentally sensitive taxation issues. The idea is not all bad. Were it not for the fact that the hon. member would move the entire federal government taxation structure in the direction of the environment, I think that some of his ideas certainly bear watching although I am not sure they would bear scrutiny.
Supply
In any event, Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw your atention to the comprehensive strategy that the government addressed in the Throne Speech in April, in which it talked about five significant directions. One direction was financial integrity, solvency and fulfilling our fiscal responsibility to future generations. I believe that the goods and services tax is a progressive tax, one that raises funds with the growth of our economy, with the growth and spending of our nation, and that we are addressing financial integrity.
The second direction is economic growth, the creation of jobs, regional development, and I think we are addressing that.
A third strategic direction is national unity, one proud country. We are addressing that in a number of ways.
The fourth is the environmental imperative, the search for sustainable development in almost all that we do. We are certainly addressing that today. This motion and its emphasis in those directions is valuable for debate in this House.
Lastly, the Throne Speech spoke about a caring and compassionate society. I think that the goods and services tax speaks to that subject. The goods and services tax is not just a new source of revenue. The goods and services tax is an effort to change the burden of taxation, to shift the emphasis from those who are unable to pay to those who are better able to pay. The goods and services tax does that in a number of ways. It does it by eliminating and maintaining the elimination of taxation on food. It does it by providing a goods and services tax credit to low-income families. It does it be integrating effectively with the income tax system. It does it by replacing the federal sales tax which is a very bad tax and which has inhibited many of the progressive measures we would like to take, including those in the environment. The goods and services tax is an instrument of social change, an instrument of shifting the burden of financial support of government administration and government efforts from those at the low-income levels to those who are able to pay. I submit that the goods and services tax is an essential instrument of both financial responsibility and financial fairness.
When we address the environment in Canada, we have to think about some of the geographic facts, some of the economic facts and some of the demographic facts of our nation. For example, one in three Canadian workers is employed directly or indirectly in resource based activities. These activities count for one half of our export

October 31, 1989
Supply
earnings. That is not an area that we can deal with frivolously in a quick fix green tax approach.
Canada has one of the world's longest coastlines, I guess the world's longest coastline of about 29,000 kilometers. We cannot deal with that on a user-pay, quick-fix green tax basis. Canadians are responsible for nearly 8 per cent .of the world's total volume of fresh water lakes. We cannot administer those on a quick-fix green tax basis.
Our country has some of the planet's largest stretches of productive farmlands and forests, and we cannot manage those on a quick-fix green tax basis. Beyond any kind of economic ties, the quality and diversity of Canada's natural resources, our parks, our mountains, our forests, our wheat fields, our rugged coastlines, undeniably shape our self-identity, our sense of Cana-dianism and shape our thoughts about how the rest of the world thinks of us. We certainly cannot address our statement of nationhood on one quick-fix green tax basis.
In light of those considerations, it is hardly surprising that Canada was an early and strong supporter of the Brundtland Commission on Environment and Development. Indeed, it is fair to say that the Brundtland commission served as a catalyst for changes that were already under way in Canada.
I have invited the hon. member for Skeena a couple of times now to visit New Brunswick and to get New Brunswick forestry legislation straight in his mind. He would discover that it, conceived in the early years of this decade, was moving in the direction of sustainable development. We are going to get him down there some day soon and set him straight. We may even get him to change his political loyalties, because sooner or later, he is going to realize that if he really wants to participate in progress in this country, he is going to have to join another team.
Canada has embraced the sustainable development credo as much as any other nation. We are working in all sectors to help put that philosophy into practice, and Canada's actions have come in a number of areas. We have established a national round table on environment and the economy, chaired by Dr. David Johnson, principal of McGill University. We have passed a new Environmental Protection Act. We will be introducing new
legislation to protect our water resources and for stricter control of toxic chemicals. Under this government's environmental choices program, we are providing seals of approval to products so that the consumer can make the right environmental choice. In 1988, this government made major amendments to the National Parks Act and moved to establish six new national parks.
All of these actions and more illustrate the movement from the old environmental agenda to the new one. The development of a comprehensive environmental agenda does not involve a single initiative. It cannot be solved by a single quick-fix green tax but by a series of purposeful steps of which the tax reform which we are presently debating and introducing in this country is a major pillar. From being simply a regulator, we must become a leader.
From simply treating symptoms, we must deal with the causes and the solutions. From merely acting in isolation, we must build partnerships.
Regulation remains an important element of our environmental policy tool kit, and Canada has recently adopted a new environmental law, the Canadian Environmental Protection Act. Nevertheless, Canadians also recognize that regulation alone will not achieve sustainable development. Governments, industry, communities, and individuals must demonstrate leadership within their own spheres of influence.
This government has moved quickly to establish innovative decision-making approaches that institutionalize sustainable development and make it part of the every day process. Some of those recent developments include a new federal cabinet structure that gives prominence to the environment, a new environment committee of cabinet that has been established to provide leadership in ensuring that all federal policies and programs take environmental factors into consideration.
The Standing Committee on the Environment, of which members of all parties in this House participate, has demonstrated leadership in the care it has taken to select its program for a study and a report on atmospheric pollution in the context of sustainable development with respect to global warming. A federal environmental assessment review process has been established which will have a legislative underpinning, a state of the environment reporting system, development of conservation strategies in the areas of waterfowl habitat and

wetland preservation, fish habitat maintenance, and efforts in the forestry sector.
The second major step in meeting the new agenda is shifting from treating symptoms to dealing with root causes and solutions. No one can ignore, for example, accidents or spills when they occur. Yet the cliche is true, it is cheaper to prevent than to clean up. Sustainable development imposes this attitude as a necessary condition.
The third element is the shift from acting in isolation to building partnerships. The government has created round tables on the environment and the economy to bring these two important decision-making perspectives together among government, industry, labour, science, and citizen groups. They are to serve as permanent mechanisms for exchanging concerns, finding areas of common ground and seeking approaches that are understood and respected by all sides.
Canadians are building partnerships in other forums as well. Industry and consumer groups are co-operating to establish an environmentally friendly products labelling system so that consumers can make informed choices in their purchases. Environmental interest groups are working with governments to increase public awareness about acid rain and other environmental problems such as the ozone layer and global warming.
These domestic initiatives will help establish sustainable development in Canada. The actions in effect will help put our own house in order. The government is dedicated to taking clear and decisive leadership on the environment in partnership with all Canadians. It has taken mankind a great deal of its history to realize that we the people are really the cause of the ecological crisis of unprecedented proportions which we are now facing. We in this government have decided to act.
In the Speech from the Throne, we committed ourselves to a vision of a nation living in harmony with the environment and one that will co-operate with other nations to establish and achieve sustainable development
Supply
on a global scale. This mission demands that all of our energies be directed toward that goal.
The key word is still development. We must create new capacity to feed our human populations which will double on this earth in the next 50 years. We must create new energy sources and new energy capability five times the present capacity, according to the Brundtland Commission, just to be able to create and sustain the development of our emerging population.
The aim of this House must be, as the previous speaker said, to rise in a non-partisan way above political posturing and to take real and constructive action. We have the opportunity to join peoples from all regions, young and old, men and women, in a common cause. We have among us the talents and the energies to demonstrate that we deserve the trust of future generations to protect and to preserve their interests. We must move beyond debates of simple answers to complex problems and get on with the development and the implementation of a comprehensive environmental agenda.
This motion, as well-intentioned as it may be in an environmental sense, is really an exercise in quick-fix simplicity, a user-pay guide to environmental sustainability. That, with respect, Mr. Speaker, simply will not work.
I will be voting against this motion.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ken James (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the fundamental objective of the tax system is to raise revenue, to finance the provision of a Public Service and to service the public debt. The tax system should be fair and efficient and it should not distort economic decisions in an undesirable direction.
This motion would have the House make major changes to the tax system, including the corporate income tax system, so that its fundamental objective would be to achieve a quite different goal. While it is a laudable goal, I would question whether the taxation system should be so changed. Rather, we should continue the process of tax reform initiated by the government in order to build a sound, reliable and fair tax system. Only then should consideration be given to using it to achieve goals such as that proposed in today's motion.

October 31, 1989
Supply
The corporate tax system that existed when this government came to office in 1984 was seriously in need of overhaul. A host of special deductions, exemptions and credits had seriously eroded the tax base. Many of these incentives had been put in place for what would appear to be exemplary reasons; for example, job creation, economic growth and the expansion of research and development. But their existence forced tax rates to be increased to generate the necessary revenue.
Moreover, the results being achieved by the combination of generous incentives to direct corporate behaviour and high tax rates is well known to all members, including members of the opposition.
Many profitable corporations were non-taxpaying. Corporate tax revenues were low and there was little evidence that the measures were achieving the desired objectives. Numerous schemes to further reduce corporate taxes were being developed by aggressive tax planners seeking to get the most out of these measures. It is extremely useful to look at this experience and the results of the corporate tax reform when considering the wholesale introduction of tax incentives or penalties to achieve other eminently desirable objectives. Preservation of the environment is an objective, of course, which we all support.
As the Minister of Finance emphasized in his speech to the Commonwealth Finance Ministers meeting in September, the environment is an area where changes in policy are essential. This presents a great challenge to governments in Canada and elsewhere in the world. Managing changes in policies to achieve the best results with minimal adverse side effects are as important here as in other areas of economic management.
The corporate tax system is one part of the tax system where there has been substantial change and experimentation in recent decades. It is instructive to look at it as an example of the constraints that arise. As I noted, the corporate tax system which this government inherited was widely considered a failure. Substantial corporate resources were being used, not to create real economic benefits, but rather to generate tax benefits, and the objectives of growth and job creation were not being achieved.
Equally disturbing was the fact that the generosity of these special incentives led to their growing year after year at a faster rate than could possibly be used. Intricate mechanisms were designed to use losses against income from unrelated activities.
Faced with the situation the government made a fundamental choice. It did not adopt a quick-fix solution with an appealing name. It developed a careful analysis of the problems of the system and the direction and changes that should move the system.
Following the release and public response to a discussion paper in 1985 outlining this analysis, proposals for change were put forward as part of a tax reform. The changes were balanced in nature, recognizing the factors that bear on the system. Taxes were raised by some $1 billion annually from the corporate sector. Tax rates were designed to keep us internationally competitive. The base was broadened to reduce the list of profitable non-taxpaying firms. Perhaps most importantly, the system was redirected so that economic, not tax factors, were at the base of the corporate decisions.
The steps taken in line with this over-all strategy have extended well beyond tax reform itself and include measures taken throughout the government's mandate. The first step was the moratorium on scientific research tax credits, that prime example of a wasteful and ill-conceived incentive, albeit directed at an important objective, R and D.
Other steps include measures to prevent a variety of schemes to transfer tax losses from non-profitable corporations to profitable corporations; the reduction of the accelerated capital consumption allowance rates across a broad range of capital goods and industries; the elimination of the general investment tax credits which proved to be such a failure in producing real wealth; the reduction of a variety of special purpose investment tax credits; an increase in the rate of taxation of capital gains; the introduction of a corporate surtax; the introduction of put-in-use rules to limit the use of deductions where taxable income is not forthcoming; removal of inventory allowance; curtailment of the use of leasing to transfer benefits for accelerated capital consumption allowances from non-taxable entities to profitable firms; and a creditable tax on large deposit-taking institutions.

Most recently, a large corporations tax has been adopted to ensure that all large companies contribute to deficit reduction. This tax, of course, will add almost $1 billion dollars to the debt control effort.
These changes were fundamental and their benefit has been significant. We have a broader and more stable corporate tax base which ensures that corporations, and especially large corporations, pay their fair share. They had not done this in the past. In total, these measures add some $2 billion annually to corporate tax revenues and, just as important, it directs attention back to the basic economic fundamentals.
I have not listed these serious problems of the past and the major effort that has been made to correct them to imply that tax changes should not be used to support desirable objectives such as environmental policy. Rather, I have set them out to show what serious problems can arise if wholesale measures are adopted without recognition of the limits on the tax system's ability to deliver. Let us not revisit the mistakes of the 1970s in the name of environmental policy.
I appreciate the opportunity to bring some of this information to the attention of the House today as we consider the motion of the member opposite, which is about adding a new tax for environmental purposes.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak in favour of this motion. Since I was elected a number of people have asked me, of all the things that we deal with in Parliament, what really are the significant issues. I started off by thinking that when it really comes down to it, there are probably only three overriding issues that are particularly significant to the next generation. The first is peace and the question of disarmament, because without that, the next generation is not going to be here.
The second is the question of poverty and the distribution of wealth, not only within Canada, but on a world-wide basis. Canada is starting to create a whole class of poor people; 1.2 million children live in poverty. In the world, we have a severe problem of economic wealth on the one hand and abject poverty, starvation and death on the other.
The third issue is the question of the protection of the environment and sustainable development. In many ways, these issues are rolled up into one. Certainly peace and disarmament is going to mean less use of materials
Supply
that are involved in the pollution of the environment and that will allow us to deal with the question of income and poverty. I think there is an interrelationship between those three issues.
The environment is one issue on which this government does not seem to be leading the way. There is far more acceptance in Canada of strong measures to deal with the question of the degradation of our environment than this government is prepared to deal with.
I just want to remind government members of what the Secretary General of the United Nations Commission said about this government. "The federal government is long on talk and short on action when it comes to cleaning up the environment. Canada is a country noted for leading with rhetoric and following others with action". Again that is what is being discussed here, when the people on the other side say that a green tax is not a feasible way to change the way we relate to our environment.
Let me talk a bit about the whole question of what is the purpose of taxation. Hon. members on the other side of the House indicate that the raising of taxes is simply a matter of raising money. If that were true, then I would think they would simply raise the money from those who could most afford it. They use tax for social policy. They have consciously shifted the tax burden from corporations to individual families. That is a social policy. That has nothing to do with raising revenue. This country has gone from corporations paying 50 per cent of the tax down to them paying 20 per cent.
The GST is as much a direct social policy as it is a method of raising money. There are many ways that the government could raise money and what it is choosing is a regressive tax.
One speaker said this afternoon that corporations only use pure economic considerations and that is what we should do in making decisions about taxation. Most big corporations do make pure economic decisions, and if they can get away with polluting because it is simply cheaper, they will do so. There are many large corporations, including Cominco, that consider fines almost like a licence to pollute, simply because it is less expensive than putting in proper scrubbing or air pollution equipment.

October 31, 1989
Supply
In this country, we have allowed the companies to make the economic decisions that are best for them, and we pick up half the costs. For example, do we bill McDonald's for disposing of all their garbage? The cost to the whole community for cleaning up pollution, dealing with garbage and a deteriorating environment is very, very expensive. Yet we have told companies that we will pick up that cost so they can become profitable. The total community is subsidizing that industry through taxation.
The other thing I hear a lot about from government members is the discussion about reducing the deficit and the debt. I think it is time someone went back to basic business school and started looking at what is involved with debt. Debts include assets. This government has reduced a lot of its deficit by getting rid of some of its best assets like Air Canada. It has given away our assets.
When one starts looking at debts, one has to look at accounts payable. Any corporation at the end of the year has to take into consideration accounts payable. What we have done as a society is create an accounts payable for our children in environmental damage that is horrendous. Right now, in order to allow a big corporation to make a little bit more profit today, we are transferring the debt to our children. I think it is time that some of the people over there not only learn a little bit about the environment but learn a little bit about basic economics and how a balance sheet reads.
In Surrey we have a number of environmental problems. The whole question of the use of landfill as a dump has been very difficult for the Greater Vancouver Regional District to deal with.
In the last year, Surrey went into a recycling program. Initially people thought it might be done as cheaply as $4 per household. It has turned out to cost $15 per household. Let me tell you, most people are quite willing to pay an additional $15.
As they brought in the blue boxes, they were surprised at the extent of their use within the community. Eighty per cent of the households are now using the blue boxes. This has already meant a 16 per cent reduction in the use of the landfill, and that is only with part of the municipality participating.
Also, the volume of tonnage going into the blue boxes and being recycled is much greater than we had anticipated. In fact, in Surrey, out of the first 36,000 homes, we
are collecting more recyclable materials than is now being collected from 67,000 homes in Edmonton.
We are now seeing that individuals are willing to change their behaviour to become environmentally responsible and are also willing, at the local level, to pick up some of the costs. They are quite prepared to pay through their municipal taxes additional money to allow recycling.
The government does not seem to realize that Canadians are quite prepared to pay through a tax system in order to bring about environmental clean-up. I refer to a survey which showed that two-thirds of Canadians would accept a five cent a litre pollution tax on gasoline if the money would be turned back into air pollution control. Six out of ten Canadians would pay 10 per cent on energy consumption in order to promote conservation. Two-thirds of Canadians would accept a 50 per cent increase in the cost of garbage collecting, not just a minor increase, but 50 per cent, if there was a recycling program involved.
The Canadian public is more than willing to start to look at not only their individual behaviour but their tax base as it relates to the environment. We now have to bring in a green tax that will do two or three specific things, particularly as it relates to large corporations. It will provide us with some revenue that would allow us to monitor environmental impact. It would provide us with some funds for cleaning up the environment. It would also allow us funds for research because the new technologies are what we are going to have to develop if we are going to get control over our environment.
Many of the processes we are now using simply are not environmentally sound, but there is no incentive for corporations to do new research if they can get away with using the old technology. We need an environmentally sound green tax that would collect money so we could do things like monitor, clean up and research. It would also give an incentive to users and corporations so it would be more to their economic advantage to change their methods of production and to change their ways of interacting with the environment.
I would like to talk briefly about one of the things that we have to do in the area of carbon fuels. That is one of the major areas where, if there was motivation, government leadership and a proper green tax, we could reduce our carbon fuel use by at least 50 per cent. This would have a significant impact on global warming and on the
October 31, 1989

quality of air plus on the reduction of a limited resource, our fossil fuels.

Mr. Speaker, I want to say how much I appreciate your recognizing me today to speak on what is a very historic debate. I think that we will look back in years hence and say that this was the day that the House of Commons really began addressing the serious environmental and ecological issues facing not only the country but indeed the planet.
I am pleased to participate in today's debate sponsored by the hon. member for Skeena, the New Democratic Party's environment spokesperson, who moved that this House call upon the government to implement an ecologically sound green tax system.
We sometimes ask what the point of the tax system is, and I think it is fundamentally twofold. One is naturally to obtain revenues for the federal government to enable it to serve the people of Canada in a variety of ways. But the tax system also does other things. It certainly shapes consumer demand, and that is what we are talking about to a certain extent today.
We are most familiar, in times past, with what we called the sin taxes. We would jack up the prices on beer, wine, spirits, and cigarettes, presumably not only to generate revenue but also to encourage people not to use these sin products with the assumption that if the price is high enough people will have second thoughts and realize that not only are these products bad for their health, they are also very expensive.
We also encourage corporate behaviour. We, as a matter of fact, lose billions of dollars each year through our tax system as we encourage companies to locate in certain areas, to invest in certain types of activities, to introduce new plants and equipment, and to conduct various research and development programs. We use the tax system not only to shape consumer demand but also to shape corporate behaviour.
In that respect my hon. friend from Skeena has introduced to us now an approach to use our tax system to encourage not only consumers, but corporations as well, to behave in ways that are environmentally friendly.
Supply
He has referred to the green tax system or the GTS as opposed to the GST, the goods and services tax, which my hon. colleague has pointed out adequately was veiy regressive not only in terms of taxing the lower income people at essentially a much higher rate than the upper income earners but also in terms of the environment.
As my hon. friend from Skeena pointed out, the taxes on recycled paper are the same as on unrecycled paper, bicycles are taxed at the same rate as large automobiles, canoes are taxed at the same rate as luxury motor boats, and alternative energy is taxed at the same rate as fossil fuels. This simply shows that as a Parliament we do not distinguish in our tax system between those activities and those products that are environmentally friendly and those that are environmentally unfriendly. The green tax system would differentiate clearly between these types of products and their related behaviour.
I cannot help but bring to the House's attention the fact that Margaret Thatcher, who I suspect is no friend to the environment in many ways, saw the need to introduce a lower tax on unleaded gasoline. Within the year following that tax measure unleaded gasoline tripled its market share which of course resulted in health benefits for British children. Probably a lot of young children are alive today simply as a result of this one measure that encouraged people to use unleaded gasoline. I hate to think for a moment that Margaret Thatcher is ahead of us as a country in terms of dealing with environmental issues. That is why I am so pleased to participate in this historic debate today calling for a GTS, a green tax system, as opposed to the goods and services tax initiative.
I think it is important to recognize that we do not have years and years to deal with the environmental catastrophe that presently faces us. It is happening around us as we speak. There will be cataclysmic implications unless dramatic action is taken. To create a Department of the Environment and so on, to go out to have a look after a major spill has occurred or major toxic wastes has been dumped into a river system, to say "naughty, naughty", to slap somebody on the wrist and to impose a small fine is obviously an approach of the past tense. No longer can we afford to approach the challenges in this way.

October 31, 1989
Supply
That is why this green tax system is so important, because it would reflect the environmental cost of manufacturing a product, for example. Such a tax system would reflect the cost to the environment of dumping toxic substances into lakes and rivers and the cost of dumping chemical waste down river banks and in landfill sites.
To look at something very specific to those of us from British Columbia, those forest companies which are investing in practices that result in sustainable development would be taxed at a different level than those corporations which are involved in practices that are obviously resulting in the deterioration, decline, and destruction of our forest resources. We will say to those companies that that type of corporate behaviour is unacceptable and consequently they will be taxed at a much higher rate than the company that is very environmentally sensitive and is conducting silviculture and reforestation practices at a very sophisticated level to ensure that the forest resource is maintained in perpetuity.
We will be able to reward, on the one hand, and say to those who simply ignore the environmental and ecological implications of their corporate behaviour that this is something that we are not going to accept and they will be paying taxes to compensate accordingly.
Obviously, the green tax system would be used to promote and encourage recycled products. Those manufacturers who use new resources, especially non-renewable resources, would be taxed for these while other manufacturers who use reused resources would benefit. This is one way that we can indicate how serious we are as a Parliament in encouraging those manufacturers that would be open to using recycled material.
Of course, this idea that we can recycle is not a new idea. After all, we do make it financially attractive so that certain companies will recycle copper, batteries, bottles and so on. But we need to extend this to a much greater extent to encourage those firms which it will actually in most cases cost more money to participate in using recycled material. They can be compensated for those additional costs at least in the beginning, by a revised tax system. In that way we will be encouraging those environmentally and ecologically sensitive manufactures.
Under a green tax system styrofoam egg cartons would have an extra tax to reflect the waste that is created in the manufacturing of styrofoam, paid for by the manufacturer, as well as the cost of safely disposing them, which is now paid by the consumer. Again the tax system would be modified so that the users of styrofoam, the manufacturers of styrofoam products and so on, would again be paying a different tax from those who are using products that are much environmentally sound.
I must say that I do not feel comfortable making that statement knowing that in our own lobbies here on Parliament Hill and in the restaurants we are drinking beverages from styrofoam cups. While we speak today we ought to be cleaning up, in our own lobby, to indicate at least some sensitivity even here.
Sticking to the egg carton example, egg cartons that a manufacturer would make out of recycled pulp would be tax exempt or would be taxed at a significantly lower level. Or, perhaps an incentive could be built into the corporate tax system that would require them to use these types of these recycled materials.
We can refer of course to the need to have a carbon tax, recognizing that carbon emissions are very serious polluters in many ways. Not only are the carbon emissions contributing to the greenhouse effect, but carbon emissions combine with sunlight to produce ground level ozone which has serious implications and impact on the health of Canadians. A carbon tax would recognize the heavy cost to the environment of burning fossil fuels. Such a tax would encourage energy conservation and raise revenues for research and development of alternative energy sources.
When we look at what other countries do we see that we are quickly falling behind countries that already have modified their tax systems to fend off the impending global catastrophe. Sweden taxes the active ingredients in pesticides and fertilizers and batteries containing mercury and cadmium. Italy taxes plastic bags. Finland and Norway tax non-returnable containers. Japan, West Germany and Switzerland charge higher landing fees for large, noisy and polluting aircraft.
In our own country those people who choose a smaller fuel efficient car should be taxed on that vehicle at a much lower rate than those people who, for whatever reason, choose a large gas guzzling car, again contribut-
October 31, 1989

ing much more in terms of environmental deterioration than the person driving a energy efficient vehicle.
One could go on and on in terms of the details that a green tax would incorporate.
I simply want to say that I feel, as I am sure do all the others who participated in this debate and the people who have listened to the debates, that today may be a turning point in that this is the first time such a discussion has occurred in Parliament in terms of using our tax system to motivate Canadians, to motivate the corporate sector to behave in different ways that would be more in tune with a clean environment.
As I say, we do not have ten years to work this out. We do not have five years to discuss this matter. We must move with haste and we must encourage people, not only in Parliament but beyond, to do what we can together to ensure that such a tax system is implemented as quickly as possible.
I give great credit to my hon. colleague for Skeena for initiating the discussion today and introducing a lot of us to the possibility of a green tax system.

Mr. Speaker, first of all I would like to thank my colleagues for the debate on this topic. I think it is a legitimate topic. It is very topical, if you will; with the times.
I would also like to say what a great opportunity this is for Canadians to look at the option of taxing in the area of environmentally unsound products. I would like to address my question to my friend in the area of agriculture. Within the Similkameen Valley in particular we have what is euphemistically called organic farming. It, of course, uses no pesticides, no herbicides, and no chemically produced fertilizers.
In an area in the Okanagan and throughout the Similkameen Valley where a lot of those products have been used over a good number of years in the agricultural community, we have high levels of phosphates in our water systems and we are in the process of looking at methods of cleaning it up.
It seems to me that the area of organic farming is an area that should be looked at. Does my colleague see a green tax as a way of encouraging research in the area of
Supply
organic farming and, in fact, encouraging farming methods that will be environmentally friendly?

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate my hon. friend's very thoughtful question. I must say that he has touched an area that a lot of us have spent a lot of time thinking about in the last little while, that is, how to encourage the use of organically grown food that is pesticide-free in terms of residue.
I think it is fair to say that at the moment, unfortunately, those foods that are most ecologically sound often cost more because of the way they are grown and the intensive labour involved and so on. I think this green tax provides us with an incredible opportunity to send a very clear signal to those firms, large or small, and those individuals who are presently involved in organic food production, to give them encouragement and provide a tax system that would encourage the development of organic food production and, quite the contrary, increase taxes on those foods that are saturated with herbicides, pesticides and fertilizers of one kind or another.
That is exactly what the consuming public is saying. It is prepared to pay a slightly higher cost, but I think we can do our role by changing our tax system to give all the encouragement possible to develop organic food free of pesticide residues.
I appreciate the comments of my hon. friend who represents part of the Okanagan Valley because I know in his constituency there are a number of individuals who are actively involved. If there is some way we could provide them with encouragement, that would be very satisfying indeed for all of us.
